pages.title: KDataForge
pages.description: Install, create, and extend YAML content packs for Satisfactory.

sections.heading: KDataForge
sections.text: KDataForge loads YAML packs that change or add Satisfactory content at runtime. Choose the path that matches what you need to do.

sections.heading: I use packs
sections.text: Start with the Player guide. It explains how to install, update, remove, and troubleshoot a pack without requiring YAML or Unreal Engine knowledge. For multiplayer, install the same pack versions on the host or dedicated server and every client. Each game process loads its own files. KDataForge does not transfer packs, compare checksums, or reject mismatched pack sets during connection.

sections.heading: I create YAML packs
sections.text: Follow Create your first pack to make one visible recipe change and verify it in game. Continue with the How-to guides when you have a specific goal, such as adding an item and recipe, localizing a pack, or integrating another mod. Open Authoring concepts for the pack, document, target, operation, identity, reload, multiplayer, and tool-choice model. Then use Document types and authoring features for the capability you need. The Examples provide complete packs, while the Reference holds exact fields, defaults, constraints, and API contracts. Before distributing a pack, run Lint your pack. KDataForgeJS adds typed TypeScript for computed values, Blueprint hooks, delegates, and runtime decisions. Start with TypeScript scripting with KDataForgeJS, then open the guide for setup, reflection, lifecycle, content authoring, or runtime limits.

sections.heading: I develop native mods or KDataForge
sections.text: Start with the Native developer guide for module dependencies, registration timing, and a minimal handler. Use Contributor internals for the runtime pipeline, persistence model, multiplayer boundaries, and module layout. Native extension points live in API design and the handler template. The UE editor integration documents KDF.ApplyToAssets.

sections.heading: Runtime tools
sections.text: | Command | Where | What it does | | /kdf report | Chat | Shows detected packs, applied documents and operations, warnings, and errors. | | /kdf reload | Host or dedicated-server administrator chat | Rescans and reapplies packs in that game process after initial loading. Run /kdf report afterward. | | KDF.Reload | Host or server console | Runs the same reload and writes its summary to the log. | | /kdf config dump|set|apply | Chat; writes require host or dedicated-server administrator | Inspects, stages, and applies pack settings. | | /kdf editor | Chat; opens a host-local UI | Requests the in-game editor for live property edits, pack authoring, undo and redo, and YAML export. This branch has no host/admin permission check. | | /kdf sound <PackRef> <Id> | Local player controller | Previews a generated sound on that machine. | | KDF.Editor | Console | Runs the same editor toggle. | | /kdf debug on|off | Chat | Enables or disables global debug logging. With no argument, it toggles the current state. | | KDF.Debug 1 | Console or -KDFDebug launch argument | Logs one [KDF DEBUG] line for each applied operation, including editor edits. | | KDF.ApplyToAssets [PathFilter] | Unreal Editor console only | Applies supported YAML patches to editor assets and marks their packages dirty. | See Commands and console variables for every chat, runtime console, reflection, and Unreal Editor command, including permissions and process boundaries. Reload is process-local. Frozen registrations, irreversible world changes, properties classified as cold, and packs that generate native CDO helper assets still require a restart. While native helper assets are active, KDataForge refuses manual and automatic reload before restoring properties.

pages.title: Contributor internals
pages.description: Understand KDataForge's runtime pipeline, persistence model, multiplayer boundaries, and modules.

sections.heading: Contributor internals
sections.text: This section explains why KDataForge behaves as it does and how its runtime modules work together. Pack authors do not need it for routine YAML work. Read it when you are designing around load order, save identity, reload limits, or multiplayer, or when you are adding a native handler. - Architecture follows a document from filesystem discovery through YAML parsing, fixed-stage application, reflection-based property edits, generated-content persistence, reload, and the current multiplayer boundary. - Module structure maps the runtime modules, their source layout, and their dependency rules. Those boundaries keep public integration contracts separate from parsing, reflection export, runtime application, and user-interface code. Use API design for the supported native integration surface and the handler template when implementing a document type.

pages.title: Architecture
pages.description: System design, data flow, subsystems, savegame persistence strategy, and current multiplayer boundaries.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: KDataForge is a data-driven runtime content editing framework. Pack authors and other mods describe changes to game content in YAML documents. The initial load parses, validates, and applies those documents before a world or save loads. A later /kdf reload restores captured baselines, rescans the packs, and runs the applicable pipeline again. Frozen registrations, irreversible world changes, and explicitly cold data still require a session restart. Authors use <your-mod>/DataForge/**/*.yml. The scanner itself starts at the Unreal project root, which is FactoryGame/ in a packaged game. It recognizes directories named DataForge, the legacy name data-editor, and any directory containing pack.yml. Roots may nest, and each YAML file is assigned only to its deepest enclosing root. An implicit pack ref and name come from the detected root's parent directory, so an explicit stable ref is recommended. Directories named Docs or Scripts, and dot-prefixed directories, are excluded from root discovery and document collection so documentation examples and cached backups cannot become active packs. !KDataForge runtime architecture from pack discovery through staged reflection operations and per-world actor patches

sections.heading: Lifecycle integration with SML
sections.text: KDataForge hooks SML's module lifecycle via two auto-discovered root modules, UKDFGameInstanceModule and UKDFWorldModule. UKDFGameInstanceModule acts across three phases. During CONSTRUCTION, its built-in handlers exist (the subsystem's Initialize), and this is the window in which third-party mods register their own handlers. During INITIALIZATION, UKDFSubsystem::RunInitialLoad() performs the full scan, parse, and apply pass. This runs before any world or save loads, so CDO edits and generated classes exist before anything references them. This initial pre-world pass runs once per GameInstance; later reloads use the reload path and retain the cold boundaries described below. During POST_INITIALIZATION, the load report is logged. UKDFWorldModule runs per world. It registers the /kdf chat command. During world INITIALIZATION, after save deserialization and before actor BeginPlay, it drains queued content registration, applies schematic/research registry removals, then asks UKDFContentRemoveSubsystem to sweep save-restored recipes. Registration runs first, so an explicit removal wins when both name the same class. SML guarantees all modules receive CONSTRUCTION before any receives INITIALIZATION, which makes the third-party handler registration window safe.

sections.heading: Core components
sections.text: | Component | Type | Responsibility | | UKDFSubsystem | GameInstanceSubsystem | Owns loader, handler registry, class/object caches, patch records, registrations, removals, and world rules | | FKDFPackScanner | static | Filesystem discovery (pruned recursive walk, pack.yml manifests) | | FKDFYamlParser | static (KDataForgeYaml) | ryml façade, the only YAML entry point; thread-safe parse, deterministic hand-written emitter | | FKDFConditionEvaluator | static | Document conditions: evaluation | | FKDFPropertyResolver | static | Property path → (FProperty, value ptr) resolution incl. containers and object dereference | | FKDFValueCodec | static | Bidirectional YAML ↔ FProperty conversion | | FKDFOpEngine | static | The 25 property operations with a per-kind capability matrix | | FKDFVanillaCache | member of subsystem | First-write snapshots for editor diff, undo, and changes-only export | | FKDFDynamicContentRegistry | member of subsystem | Creates deterministic generated classes/assets and reconstructs missing generated classes as tombstones | | UKDFCdoHandler | handler (cdo) | CDOs, data-asset instances, allAssetsOfClass, tag matcher, actor patches | | UKDFSublevelHandler | handler (sublevel) | Blocks RefinedRDLib/KBFL sublevel descriptor assets during CDOChanges | | UKDFContentClassHandler | handler base | Generates item/resource/building/unlock/recipe/schematic/research classes; queues registration/removal | | UKDFAssetHandler | handler (asset) | Decodes pack-relative 2D images into transient texture assets | | UKDFDataAssetHandler | handler (dataasset) | Creates UDataAsset instances, applies instanced lists, and requests optional consumer rescans | | UKDFCurveHandler | handler (curve) | Creates or edits UCurveFloat and UCurveVector assets during the Assets stage | | UKDFGameTagHandler | handler (gametag) | Runtime gameplay tag registration | | UKDFLocalizationHandler | handler (localization)| Runtime namespace/culture text registration | | UKDFSinkPointsHandler | handler (sinkpoints) | Queues per-world AWESOME Sink table values | | UKDFResourceNodeHandler | handler (resourcenode)| Registers descriptor/node-type purge rules for live worlds | | UKDFActorPatchSubsystem | WorldSubsystem | Applies actor patches at world begin play + every spawn | | UKDFContentRemoveSubsystem | WorldSubsystem | Orchestrates recipe sweeps and exposes per-world removal queries/counts | | UKDFResourceNodeSubsystem | WorldSubsystem | Purges matching nodes, local mesh actors, scanner data, and radar/scanner caches | | FKDFRecipeRemoval | static/native hooks | Blocks future recipe adds and removes recipes restored from server save data | | UKDFConfigRegistry | GameInstance object | Owns generated pack settings, pending values, persistence, and apply modes | | UKDFConfigSyncSubsystem | GameInstanceSubsystem | Replicates host-controlled configuration values to multiplayer clients | | AKDFEventRuleSubsystem | ModSubsystem | Runs bounded worldReady and schematicPurchased actions and stores once-per-save state | | AKDFChatCommand | chat command | Reports, reloads, configuration, editor toggle, sound preview, and debug logging |

sections.heading: Reflection engine
sections.text: Resolution (FKDFPropertyPath → FKDFPropertyResolver) turns a parsed path such as mIngredients[0].Amount into a value, segment by segment, supporting name lookup (including Blueprint authored names), array/set index access, and map key lookup. Dereferencing through object-typed members is also supported, which is what makes mSomeComponent.Property and default subobjects reachable. Conversion (FKDFValueCodec) supports bool, all numerics, enums (typed and byte-based), FString/FName/FText (with localized key, ns, and source fields), object/class references (hard and soft), structs (native text form, map form, positional sequence form), arrays, sets, and maps, with everything else falling back to a generic text-based conversion path. This fallback is what makes "every reflectable type" honest, without needing hundreds of hand-written cases. Operations (FKDFOpEngine) validate each op against the leaf property kind before applying it: multiply on an FString produces a diagnostic, not a silent no-op. FGameplayTagContainer is special-cased so tag containers accept append/prepend/remove/clear/set with plain tag names. The full list of the 25 supported operations, their signatures, and which property kinds accept each one is covered in Operations. The property kinds themselves, and how a mIngredients[0].Amount-style path resolves, are covered in Property Types.

sections.heading: Vanilla snapshots
sections.text: Before the first write to any (object, property path) pair, the original value is exported to canonical text and stored in FKDFVanillaCache. The in-game editor uses this snapshot for its Diff tab, undo workflow, and changes-only export.

sections.heading: Runtime actor patches
sections.text: applyToSpawnedActors: true on a cdo patch registers an FKDFActorPatch. UKDFActorPatchSubsystem applies the ops to all matching pre-existing actors at world begin play, and to every matching actor the moment it spawns. This guarantees YAML values win even where per-instance state, such as save-restored values or archetypes, would override plain CDO defaults. Exact-class or subclass matching is controlled by applyToSubclasses. Actor-instance operations are direct writes. They do not compare against vanilla snapshots and do not preserve player-modified or save-restored values. The same class-scoped operation list is applied to every matching instance. The cdo document type, its properties:/applyToSpawnedActors/applyToSubclasses fields, and the CDO/data-asset/tag-matcher targeting model are covered in full in Patching (type: cdo) and Targeting.

sections.heading: Per-world registration and removal
sections.text: GameInstance handlers cannot mutate world managers because no gameplay world exists during the initial YAML pass. They retain deterministic requests instead: - recipe, schematic, and research entries queue SML content registration; - document-level remove: on those same types queues exact-class removal rules; - sinkpoints queues Sink table writes; - resourcenode queues descriptor/node-type purge rules; - cdo with applyToSpawnedActors queues actor-class patch rules. UKDFWorldModule drains registrations before removals during world INITIALIZATION. SML directly removes schematic and research classes. Recipes need FKDFRecipeRemoval: process-wide hooks block future singular and batch adds, while the per-world sweep removes recipes already restored from the server save before AFGRecipeManager::BeginPlay builds derived caches. Resource Node purges use a separate four-point schedule because level actors, streamed levels, spawns, and late descriptor retargeting become visible at different times.

sections.heading: Savegame persistence
sections.text: Dynamically created content must survive save/load with valid class paths. Class generation relies on SML's FClassGenerator::GenerateSimpleClass (root-set, parent layout copy, CDO auto-created). Class identity is id-based and deterministic: package /KDataForge/Gen/<PackRef>, class Gen_<PackRef>_<Id>. It is never derived from file paths or load order, so renaming a file must not orphan save data. Classes survive save and load because they are created during GameInstance INITIALIZATION, strictly before any save loads. The save serialiser resolves class paths through StaticFindObject before attempting a linker load, so resolution hits the in-memory class. No cooked package is needed. The constraint is that generated classes keep the parent's layout: no new reflected properties and no new components. All variation lives in CDO defaults. This covers descriptors, recipes, schematics, and unlocks fully, but it does not cover new buildables with custom components. A global generated-content manifest at Saved/KDataForge/GeneratedClasses.json records **every generated class ever created**, including its pack, id, and parent path. At startup, recorded classes missing from the current YAML are recreated as tombstones: functional but hidden and deprecated, so old saves load cleanly even after packs are removed. Because the manifest is global, class-path resolution works for any save whether or not KDataForge wrote its header. Renames use redirects: in pack.yml (OldId: NewId), which feeds FCoreRedirects so old save class paths resolve to the renamed class. Per-save state is held by AKDFStateSubsystem : AModSubsystem with SaveGame properties that store the applied-pack history: pack ref, version, and timestamp per entry. Removal features have separate persistence rules: - schematic and research-tree registry removals write nothing to the save and reverse next session after the pack is removed, but do not revoke purchases or research progress; - recipe removal mutates the saved available-recipe list, then self-heals on a later load without the pack when purchased schematics reapply unlocks; - resourcenode destroys world actors, and vanilla can persist those destruction tombstones even after the pack is removed. It is a potentially irreversible world migration. See Recipes, Schematics, Research Trees, and Resources before using those paths. See Recipes, Schematics, and Unlocks for the document types that drive this generated-class path, and Renaming Content Safely for how redirects: is used in practice.

sections.heading: Multiplayer boundaries
sections.text: Every game process performs its own initial YAML load. The current source has no pack-checksum handshake, mismatch rejection, or server-to-client operation stream. Install the same packs and versions on the server and every client. UKDFRemoteCallObject::Server_ApplySetOp is a host-gated RPC scaffold. The editor UI does not call it, and there is no general Server_ApplyOps pipeline. The /kdf editor branch itself does not run the host or administrator permission check used by reload and configuration writes. It requests the host-local editor window from the process that handles the command. Treat live editor changes as local process state, not synchronized multiplayer state.

sections.heading: Determinism rules
sections.text: 1. Stages execute in fixed EKDFStage enum order. 2. Pack dependencies are hard topological constraints. Packs with missing, self-referential, or transitively invalid dependencies are rejected. Dependency cycles are rejected. Among packs whose dependencies are ready, higher priority runs first and ref ascending breaks ties. 3. Within a stage, handlers are ordered by priority descending then root type ascending. Documents follow their dependency-ordered packs, then same-stage include: constraints and relative path. 4. Map iteration never determines apply order. FKDFNode maps preserve document order. 5. Every process must see the same pack set and inputs to produce the same result. KDataForge does not verify this across multiplayer peers yet. For the module layout that hosts these subsystems and handlers, see Module Structure. For the YAML fields that condition evaluation, targeting, and the stage/handler pipeline parse, see the YAML Schema reference.

pages.title: Module structure
pages.description: C++ module organization, folder layout, and dependency rules across KDataForge's runtime and editor modules.

sections.heading: Module structure
sections.text: YAML pack authors do not need the module details on this page. KDataForge discovers their pack files through the runtime loader. This information is for contributors to KDataForge's C++ runtime and built-in handlers, and for third-party mod authors registering a native handler for a document root type. It explains where code belongs, which dependencies it may use, and which interfaces are stable across releases. KDataForge is one Unreal plugin with five runtime modules and one Unreal Editor module. Each boundary isolates a public contract, parser dependency, reflection export workload, runtime UI, or editor commandlet.

sections.heading: Why the split exists
sections.text: Five concerns drive where a module boundary sits: - Contract isolation. Third-party mods that want to add a handler must link against something stable. Bundling that contract into the same module as the fast-moving loader/reflection internals would mean every internal refactor risks an ABI break for downstream mods. KDataForgeApi exists so that contract can stay frozen while everything else evolves underneath it. See API Design for what that contract contains. - Exception containment. The vendored YAML parser (rapidyaml) reports errors by throwing, but the rest of the codebase doesn't build with C++ exceptions enabled. Rather than flip on exceptions plugin-wide, only the module that wraps the parser does. - UI dependency isolation. The in-game editor pulls in InputCore, UMG, Slate, SlateCore, and AppFramework. Keeping it in KDataForgeEditorUI stops those dependencies from leaking into the loader/reflection runtime, even though the module itself is still declared as a Runtime module. - Reflection export isolation. Runtime and commandlet reflection exports scan large type and asset catalogs and can read texture data. KDataForgeReflection keeps that toolchain separate from normal pack loading. - Localization commandlet isolation. YAML text gathering needs Unreal Editor localization modules. KDataForgeLocalization is an Editor module, so those dependencies never enter game or dedicated-server targets.

sections.heading: The six modules
sections.text: Five modules are declared "Type": "Runtime" in the .uplugin manifest: KDataForgeApi, KDataForgeYaml, KDataForge, KDataForgeReflection, and KDataForgeEditorUI. KDataForgeLocalization is declared "Type": "Editor". The runtime also links the external KDFFlacLibrary module under Source/ThirdParty; it is a library wrapper, not one of the plugin modules listed in the manifest. That's a deliberate naming trap worth calling out. "EditorUI" refers to an in-game editor window rendered with hand-built Slate while the game is running, not to Unreal Editor-only code. Nothing in that module is gated behind WITH_EDITOR, and none of its dependencies are editor-only modules. It has to build and link cleanly anywhere the plugin loads it.

sections.heading: `KDataForgeApi` the public contract
sections.text: Third-party mods use this module for handler types and keep it intentionally tiny: Source/KDataForgeApi/Public/ ├── KDFDataEditorHandler.h ├── KDFHandlerBase.h ├── KDFNode.h ├── KDFConfigTypes.h ├── KDFTemplateProvider.h └── KDFTypes.h Its dependency list is just Core, CoreUObject, and Engine, nothing else. That's not an accident of an early prototype. It's rule #2 below: adding a dependency here is treated as an API-breaking decision, because every third-party handler mod inherits whatever this module pulls in. The types used here (FKDFNode, UKDFHandlerBase, IKDFDataEditorHandler) are covered in API design. A worked handler implementation against this exact module lives on the Handler Template page. The native template-provider contract has its own reference.

sections.heading: `KDataForgeYaml` the YAML backend
sections.text: This module exists for one reason: to keep exceptions from leaking anywhere else in the plugin. KDFYamlParser.h parses a document that throws ryml::Callbacks::error and turns it into a clean FKDFNode tree or an error string, entirely inside this module: Source/KDataForgeYaml/ ├── Public/ KDFYamlParser.h (façade the only entry point) ├── Private/ KDFYamlParser.cpp (ryml + a deterministic hand-written emitter) └── ThirdParty/ryml/rapidyaml.hpp (v0.15.2 amalgamation vendored, never edited) bEnableExceptions = true is set only in this module's .Build.cs. The reasoning is spelled out right next to it: rapidyaml reports parse errors through a callback that throws, and that has to stay contained to this wrapper. The public surface only ever returns FKDFNode trees and error strings, never a ryml type or an exception across a module boundary. Its own dependencies are Core, CoreUObject, and KDataForgeApi (for FKDFNode). Nothing pulls FactoryGame or SML in here.

sections.heading: `KDataForge` the main runtime
sections.text: This is where nearly everything lives: the loader, the reflection engine, the built-in handlers, the subsystems, and the pieces that don't get their own module because they're not a public contract, an exception boundary, or an editor-only concern. Layering inside it happens at the folder level, not via further module splits: Source/KDataForge/{Public,Private}/ ├── Reflection/ KDFPropertyPath · KDFValueCodec · KDFOpEngine · KDFVanillaCache · KDFPatchUtil ├── Loader/ KDFPackScanner · KDFConditionEvaluator · KDFLoaderTypes ├── Content/ KDFDynamicContent (class/asset generation, manifest, tombstones) · │ KDFRecipeRemoval · KDFSoundLoader · KDFSoundEvent · KDFSoundPreview ├── Config/ descriptions and widgets contract · registry · persistence · reload scheduler · │ console commands · sound options integration ├── Template/ built-in providers · expansion · configuration expressions · cold-property catalog ├── Subsystems/ KDFSubsystem · KDFActorPatchSubsystem · KDFStateSubsystem · │ KDFContentRemoveSubsystem · KDFResourceNodeSubsystem · KDFEventRuleSubsystem ├── Handlers/ KDFCdoHandler · KDFAssetHandler · KDFCurveHandler · KDFGameTagHandler · │ KDFContentClassHandler family (Class/Item/Resource/Building/Recipe/ │ Schematic/Research/Unlock) · KDFDataAssetHandler · │ KDFSinkPointsHandler · KDFLocalizationHandler · KDFSublevelHandler · │ KDFResourceNodeHandler · KDFSoundHandler · KDFCategoryReorderHandler · │ KDFEventRuleHandler ├── Commands/ KDFChatCommand ├── Module/ KDFGameInstanceModule · KDFWorldModule (SML root modules) ├── Net/ KDFRemoteCallObject (host-gated RPC scaffold) └── EditorIntegration/ KDFEditorApply (WITH_EDITOR-gated, private-only: `KDF.ApplyToAssets` console command bakes cdo documents directly onto UE-editor assets) EditorIntegration/ is the one genuinely editor-only corner of the whole plugin, and it earns that by being gated behind WITH_EDITOR at the file level rather than by living in its own module. It never ships to Shipping or dedicated-server builds, and it has no public header at all, since nothing outside this one .cpp needs to call into it. Net/ contains a host-gated Server_ApplySetOp RPC scaffold. The current editor does not call it, and there is no checksum handshake or operation stream. See the current multiplayer boundaries in Architecture. Its dependency list is the longest of the runtime core: Core, CoreUObject, Engine, Projects, Json, GameplayTags, NetCore, AssetRegistry, ImageWrapper, RenderCore, RHI, the DummyHeaders stub module, FactoryGame, and SML, plus KDataForgeApi and KDataForgeYaml. Sound loading also links KDFFlacLibrary, VorbisAudioDecoder, Wwise modules, and Unreal's Ogg, Vorbis, and VorbisFile libraries. ImageWrapper, RenderCore, and RHI back type: asset documents, turning supported 2D image files into runtime UTexture2D assets through KDFAssetHandler.

sections.heading: `KDataForgeEditorUI` the in-game editor
sections.text: Kept as its own module so Slate, UMG, and AppFramework stay isolated from the main runtime module: Source/KDataForgeEditorUI/ ├── Public/ KDFEditorSubsystem.h · KDFEditorModel.h └── Private/ SKDFEditorWindow.* · KDFEditorStyle.h (pure code-built Slate, no UMG assets) The editor window needs to read the loader's pack manifests, walk FKDFNode trees, and apply ops through the same reflection engine the runtime uses to build its Diff and Apply tabs. Because of that, it depends on all three other modules: KDataForgeApi, KDataForgeYaml, and KDataForge, alongside InputCore, UMG, Slate, SlateCore, AppFramework (for SColorPicker), AssetRegistry, FactoryGame, and SML. The wiring between this window and the runtime it edits is covered on Editor Integration.

sections.heading: `KDataForgeReflection` the export toolchain
sections.text: This runtime module owns reflection export, texture previews, the /kdf-reflection and /kdf-export chat commands, KDF.DumpReflection, validation, and the metadata export commandlet. It depends publicly on the engine, Projects, JSON, Asset Registry, FactoryGame, SML, and DummyHeaders. Its private dependencies include KDataForge, ImageCore, RenderCore, and RHI. Keeping the exporter separate lets ordinary pack loading avoid its scanning and image-export code. The output contract and recovery workflow are documented in Reflection export.

sections.heading: `KDataForgeLocalization` the editor commandlet
sections.text: This Editor module contains GatherKDataForgeTextCommandlet. It reads pack YAML during Unreal's localization workflow and depends on UnrealEd and Localization alongside the YAML and API modules. It never loads in packaged game or dedicated-server targets. The two localization paths and their source-key rules are documented in Localization.

sections.heading: Dependency graph
sections.text: Arrows below point from a module to what it depends on. KDataForgeApi has the smallest runtime footprint. Reflection and localization tooling sit beside the main runtime instead of adding their dependencies to every pack load: KDataForgeEditorUI → KDataForge, KDataForgeYaml, KDataForgeApi (+ InputCore, UMG, Slate, SlateCore, AppFramework, AssetRegistry, FactoryGame, SML) ▲ KDataForge → KDataForgeYaml, KDataForgeApi (+ Engine, Projects, Json, GameplayTags, NetCore, AssetRegistry, ImageWrapper, RenderCore, RHI, DummyHeaders, FactoryGame, SML) ▲ KDataForgeYaml → KDataForgeApi [bEnableExceptions] (+ Core, CoreUObject) ▲ KDataForgeApi (Core, CoreUObject, Engine only) KDataForgeReflection → KDataForge (+ Projects, Json, AssetRegistry, ImageCore, RenderCore, RHI, DummyHeaders, FactoryGame, SML) KDataForgeLocalization [Editor] → KDataForgeYaml, KDataForgeApi (+ Projects, UnrealEd, Localization) > Link-dependency lesson (Shipping builds): the dev-editor target resolves symbols that the modular > Shipping DLLs do not. EKeys needs InputCore, UModContentRegistry needs SML, and > FKDFYamlParser needs KDataForgeYaml. A Shipping package run is the real link check, not a > dev-editor compile.

sections.heading: Rules for contributors
sections.text: These aren't style preferences. Each one closes off a class of bug that's already bitten this plugin once: 1. ryml types never cross the KDataForgeYaml boundary. The façade returns FKDFNode trees and error strings only. Exceptions exist only inside that module, per bEnableExceptions above. 2. KDataForgeApi stays tiny and dependency-free (Core, CoreUObject, Engine). Adding a dependency there is an API-breaking decision for every third-party handler mod. Treat it as such. 3. No editor-only module dependencies anywhere. The plugin must build for Shipping and dedicated servers. Editor-only code, if ever needed, goes behind Target.bBuildEditor in .Build.cs plus WITH_EDITOR guards (see EditorIntegration/ above for the one place this already applies). 4. Handlers live in the main module or in third-party mods. Third-party handler types derive against KDataForgeApi; calling UKDFSubsystem::RegisterHandler also requires KDataForge. Handlers never include loader or scanner internals. Everything they need arrives via the context structs that the Handler Template walks through. 5. All six plugin modules share the same build settings: CppStandard = Cpp20, PCHUsage = UseExplicitOrSharedPCHs, bLegacyPublicIncludePaths = false, and the project's clang-format is enforced across all of them. For how these modules cooperate at runtime, the fixed stage pipeline, the reflection engine, and savegame persistence, see Architecture.

pages.title: Core concepts
pages.description: Understand how KDataForge finds, identifies, orders, applies, reloads, and preserves pack content.

sections.heading: Core concepts
sections.text: KDataForge reads YAML documents and applies them to Satisfactory content. A document can edit an existing object, generate content, register data with a game system, or describe a world rule. These terms appear throughout the authoring guides and reference.

sections.heading: Pack
sections.text: A pack is one detected KDataForge root and every YAML document assigned to it. Put a pack.yml manifest at that root to give the pack a stable ref, display name, version, priority, dependencies, conditions, and generated-content redirects. Treat ref as permanent after release. KDataForge uses it in generated class paths and save records. Moving a pack without an explicit ref can change its implicit identity.

sections.heading: Document and root type
sections.text: A document is one YAML map. Its type: selects the handler that understands the document. For example, type: cdo patches reflected properties, while type: recipe can generate or register a recipe. A file can contain several documents separated by ---; each document then needs its own type:. For a single-document file, a suffix such as .cdo.yml can provide the type. An explicit type: wins when both forms are present.

sections.heading: Target, property path, and operation
sections.text: A target selects the class, object, asset set, or actor set that receives a change. A property path selects the reflected value below that target. An operation says how to change the value. type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.5 Here, target selects the Iron Ingot recipe class, path selects its manufacturing duration, and multiply changes the current value instead of replacing it. KDataForge supports 25 operations. Each operation accepts specific property kinds and arguments. Use Targeting, Property types, and Operations for those contracts.

sections.heading: Entry and generated identity
sections.text: Content-creation documents contain entries with an id. KDataForge combines the pack ref and entry id into a deterministic generated path: /KDataForge/Gen/<PackRef>.Gen_<PackRef>_<Id> Other documents in the same pack can usually refer to generated content by its short id. The full path stays stable across file moves and load-order changes. Changing an id changes the generated path. Add an old-to-new mapping under redirects: in pack.yml before shipping that rename. A redirect can preserve an entry rename inside the same pack. It cannot make a changed pack ref safe. See Renaming content safely before renaming released content.

sections.heading: Conditions and dependencies
sections.text: conditions: decide whether a pack, document, or supported list entry applies in the current environment. They can test installed mods, versions, classes, configuration, sessions, advanced game settings, and user options. A failed condition skips that scope. dependencies: in pack.yml controls order between packs. include: controls order between same-pack documents in the same processing stage. These fields describe ordering, not optional compatibility. Use conditions for optional integrations.

sections.heading: Stages and deterministic order
sections.text: KDataForge groups handlers into fixed stages so prerequisites exist before consumers use them. Gameplay tags and assets must exist before later content refers to them, and world rules wait until a world exists. Inside a stage, pack dependencies, pack priority, handler priority, includes, and relative paths determine a stable order. Do not use filenames as the identity of generated content. Filenames help order documents only after stronger ordering rules have been resolved.

sections.heading: Hot, new-actor, and cold changes
sections.text: /kdf reload restores captured baselines, rescans packs, and applies the current documents in that game process. A reloadable property can update immediately. Actor defaults often affect newly spawned actors only unless the patch also targets existing spawned actors. Cold registrations, irreversible world changes, and explicitly restart-bound settings still need a session restart. Packs that generate native CDO helper assets disable live reload. Restart after changing, disabling, or removing one of those packs. KDataForge Tools for VS Code can read reload classifications from reflection data. When a feature page gives a stricter restart rule, follow that rule.

sections.heading: Saves and removal
sections.text: Generated classes use stable paths, and KDataForge recreates missing recorded classes as hidden tombstones so an old save can still resolve them. This protects class references. It does not make every gameplay change reversible. Recipe, schematic, research, actor, inventory, and resource-node changes have different save and restoration behavior. Read the removal or world-feature page before distributing a pack that removes content or changes placed world actors.

sections.heading: Multiplayer
sections.text: Every game process loads its own files. KDataForge does not transfer packs, compare pack checksums, or stream applied operations when a player joins. Install the same pack versions on the host or dedicated server and every client. Pack configuration can distinguish host-controlled synchronized gameplay values from local values. Generated audio volume controls are local to each client. Live edits made through the in-game editor stay in the process where they were made until you export and distribute them as YAML. See the player multiplayer guide and Pack configuration for the operational details.

pages.title: Complete examples
pages.description: Adapt complete packs that combine several KDataForge document types and operations.

sections.heading: Complete examples
sections.text: These examples show several document types working together in complete packs. They assume a pack root at <your-mod>/DataForge/ and some familiarity with property types, operations, targeting, and pack conditions. If you are learning the workflow, begin with Create your first pack. Use the How-to guides for a guided task and Reference for exact field definitions. For maintained packs used in a public mod, browse KPatchwork's DataForge directory. Each subdirectory is a real compatibility pack with its own pack.yml and focused YAML documents. These packs are useful examples for conditions, cross-mod targets, dependencies, and repository layout. They also follow KPatchwork's extra contribution policy, so fields such as contributer are repository requirements rather than KDataForge runtime requirements.

sections.heading: Edit existing content
sections.text: - Balancing patches existing recipes, items, resources, equipment, consumables, radioactivity, belt speed, schematics, milestones, research trees, vehicles, trains, creatures, categories, and tag-selected targets. It uses type: cdo throughout and generates no classes. - Power and machines changes power consumption, manufacturing speed, generator output, extractor cycle time, pipeline flow limits, power-storage capacity, and drone-station logistics. Its runtime actor patches also affect placed buildings.

sections.heading: Create connected content
sections.text: - A complete building follows the dependency chain from a generated buildable class through its descriptor, build recipe, production recipes, schematic, and sink points. Six files reference the class generated by the preceding file. - End-to-end pack combines an item, recipe, schematic with an inline unlock, sink points, German localization, a KAPI data asset, and a patch for another mod's data assets. It also preserves a shipped generated id with redirects:. - KAPI data assets creates every KAPI PrimaryDataAsset family supported by the example set: air collector, cleaner, modular miner, slug breeding, and extractor or resource allow-lists.

sections.heading: Build progression data
sections.text: - Delivery task trees creates a complete UKAPIDeliveryTask graph with five nodes, negative coordinates, multi-flag mParentTask values, repeated-parent thresholds, Endless fields, and a forced schematic unlock. - Removed repeat-purchase unlocks explains how to migrate an older KLib repeat-purchase reward pack to Delivery tasks. - Unlock catalogs points to the current base-game and mod unlock references and explains which one to use. For every base-game FGUnlock subclass, its properties, and its instantiation constraints, use Base-game unlock classes.

pages.title: ADA Voice-over from a WAV File
pages.description: Complete pack example that imports a PCM16 WAV, creates an ADA message, and ties it to purchasing Hub Upgrade 1.

sections.heading: ADA Voice-over from a WAV File
sections.text: This pack imports your recording through Wwise and assigns it to a new ADA message. The message becomes eligible when Hub Upgrade 1 is purchased. Triggers observe new events: use a fresh save or choose a milestone that has not been purchased yet. Previewing sound alone does not mark the ADA message as played.

sections.heading: Pack files
sections.text: DataForge/ADAExample/ pack.yml welcome.sound.yml welcome-message.dataasset.yml audio/ welcome.wav Record or export welcome.wav as PCM16 WAV , mono or stereo, 48000 Hz. Suggested spoken text: “Welcome, pioneer. Your first Hub upgrade is complete.” This is your audio file; the YAML does not synthesize speech. Keep the file below 64 MiB. pack.yml ref : ADAExample name : ADA Voice-over Example version : 1.0.0 welcome.sound.yml type : sound sounds : - id : AdaWelcome file : audio/welcome.wav name : ADA welcome volume description : Controls playback volume for the welcome message. category : Voices subCategory : ADA welcome-message.dataasset.yml type : dataasset assets : - id : WelcomeMessage class : /Script/FactoryGame.FGMessage properties : - path : mTitle value : " First upgrade complete " - path : mMessage value : " Welcome, pioneer. Your first Hub upgrade is complete. " - path : mAudioEvent value : AdaWelcome - path : mSubtitles value : - Subtitle : " Welcome, pioneer. Your first Hub upgrade is complete. " SenderClass : /Game/FactoryGame/Interface/UI/Message/Sender/Sender_ADA.Sender_ADA_C TimeStamp : 0 - path : mCanBeQueued value : true - path : mCanBeRepeated value : false - path : mBlockedByCooldown value : false - path : mPriority value : 1 - path : mTrigger value : class : /Game/FactoryGame/AvailabilityDependencies/BP_SchematicPurchasedDependency.BP_SchematicPurchasedDependency_C properties : - path : mSchematics value : - /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-1.Schematic_1-1_C - path : mRequireAllSchematicsToBePurchased value : true mAudioEvent is a soft Wwise event reference. The short ID resolves to /KDataForge/GenAssets/ADAExample.Gen_ADAExample_AdaWelcome ; the full path is equivalent. The sound loads before the message’s properties apply. The inline trigger uses the concrete availability-dependency Blueprint; the native base class is abstract. KDataForge registers generated FGMessage instances with the game’s Primary Asset Manager, as required by Satisfactory 1.2. Install the pack before loading the world. When adding a new message to a running world, restart the session so the story subsystem discovers its trigger. The example includes one ADA popup subtitle at the beginning of the recording. For longer audio, add entries to mSubtitles using Subtitle , SenderClass and TimeStamp , with timestamps in seconds matching your recording. If your game version changes the sender asset, choose its current class from the reflection catalog. The Satisfactory ADA guide explains sender and subtitle configuration.

sections.heading: Author and check in the editors
sections.text: Open the pack in the VS Code extension. Use Wwise sound wizard, or create a sound document and add AdaWelcome / audio/welcome.wav in the Sounds form. Optional UI metadata controls its label, help text and section under Options → Audio . Add the recording to audio/ , then create the dataasset document above. Run validation. Unsupported encodings and out-of-pack paths appear in Problems. Go to definition on the AdaWelcome reference should open the sound declaration. Install the complete pack, load a save, and inspect /kdf report . Run /kdf sound ADAExample AdaWelcome to hear the recording through Wwise. If this works but ADA does not speak, inspect the message’s trigger, conditions and queue state separately. Purchase Hub Upgrade 1 to check the message trigger. The in-game editor can inspect the generated message and edit its reflected properties; pack workspace also supports sound entries. After editing the recording or YAML, run /kdf reload on the host. Multiplayer clients need the same pack and recording and must reload locally or restart the session. Changes to an already played, non-repeatable message do not reset its narrative save state.

pages.title: Balancing
pages.description: Rebalance recipes, items, resources, equipment, consumables, schematics, research, categories, and belts; apply bulk edits by tag, producer, ingredient, product, name pattern, or property value.

sections.heading: Balancing
sections.text: The examples below use type: cdo documents, which can address every reflected property on every FactoryGame class. To create _new_ content, use the page for that content type: Item, Recipe, Schematic, and friends. Start at End-to-End Pack for the tied-together version. Building and machine tuning lives in Power & Machines. > ℹ️ Verify property names and asset paths against your game version. The examples on this page > use real FactoryGame properties and content paths, but game updates occasionally rename or move > them. If a target: path or property key doesn't resolve, nothing breaks, the load report tells you > exactly which patch failed (/kdf report, see > Getting Started → Troubleshooting). Confirm > the effect in-game after every patch.

sections.heading: Recipes (`UFGRecipe`)
sections.text: Every craftable recipe in the game, whether base, alternate, or buildable, is backed by a UFGRecipe class default object. This means rebalancing crafting time, ingredient ratios, or output without replacing the recipe outright is just a cdo patch against that class. The properties worth knowing are mDisplayName, mDisplayNameOverride, mIngredients, mProduct, mManufactoringDuration, mManualManufacturingMultiplier, mProducedIn, mRelevantEvents, mVariablePowerConsumptionConstant, mVariablePowerConsumptionFactor, and mGameplayTags. The patch below halves iron ingot smelting time, doubles the ore cost, adds a bonus iron plate to the output, and unlocks the recipe in the Manufacturer as well as the Smelter: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.5 mIngredients[0].Amount: 2 mProduct: $op: append value: ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronPlate/Desc_IronPlate.Desc_IronPlate_C Amount: 1 mProducedIn: $op: append value: /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/ManufacturerMk1/Build_ManufacturerMk1.Build_ManufacturerMk1_C

sections.heading: Items (`UFGItemDescriptor`)
sections.text: UFGItemDescriptor is the base class behind every stackable item in the game. It drives how the item stacks, what it burns for, how much radiation it emits, where it sorts in the build menu, and its display text. Balancing an item's inventory footprint or fuel value means patching one of mDisplayName, mDescription, mAbbreviatedDisplayName, mStackSize, mForm, mEnergyValue, mRadioactiveDecay, mCanBeDiscarded, mRememberPickUp, mResourceSinkPoints, mSmallIcon, mPersistentBigIcon, mCategory, mSubCategories, mMenuPriority, mFluidColor, mGasColor, mIsAlienItem, or mGameplayTags. The example below bumps iron ingots to the largest stack bucket, rewrites its tooltip description, and doubles the AWESOME Sink points earned for scrapping it: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties: mStackSize: SS_HUGE # EStackSize enum: SS_ONE/SS_SMALL/SS_MEDIUM/SS_BIG/SS_HUGE/SS_FLUID mDescription: key: IronIngot_Desc ns: MyPack source: Now stacks higher. mResourceSinkPoints: $op: multiply value: 2 > ⚠️ mStackSize is an enum, not a count. EStackSize has exactly six buckets > (SS_ONE…SS_HUGE, plus SS_FLUID). It isn't "items per stack" as a number, so always set it by > name. It's also cached by the engine: writing it on the CDO alone would change nothing > in-game (KBFL ships a dedicated UKBFLCDOItemStackSize helper for exactly this reason). > KDataForge handles the cache automatically. Any op that writes mStackSize on an > FGItemDescriptor-derived target also resets the descriptor's cached stack size > (mCachedStackSize), so the example above works out of the box. Two things to know: inventories > that already contain the item may need the item re-added (or a game reload) before existing > slots reflect the new limit. Also, if you use KBFL's own CDO assets for stack sizes, don't patch > the same descriptor from both sides. See > YAML Schema → Special-cased properties.

sections.heading: Resources (`UFGResourceDescriptor`) & fluids/gases
sections.text: Raw resources, fluids, and gases extend the same UFGItemDescriptor chain but add a handful of fields that only make sense for non-solid items: mForm selects solid/liquid/gas, and mFluidColor/mGasColor drive the color used for pipe contents, tank fill levels, and the resource icon in the UI. Recoloring a fluid or changing its form uses those fields directly: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/Water/Desc_Water.Desc_Water_C properties: mFluidColor: R: 20 G: 120 B: 255 A: 255 mForm: RF_LIQUID

sections.heading: Equipment & consumables (`UFGEquipmentDescriptor`, `UFGConsumableDescriptor`)
sections.text: Descriptor subclasses inherit every UFGItemDescriptor property. Equipment adds, for example, mEquipmentClass (soft class), while consumables add health and consume properties. type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Equipment/Chainsaw/Desc_Chainsaw.Desc_Chainsaw_C properties: mEnergyValue: 0

sections.heading: Removing radioactivity
sections.text: mRadioactiveDecay on the item descriptor drives the radiation emitted by held or stored items. set it to 0 on the nuclear items: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/OreUranium/Desc_OreUranium.Desc_OreUranium_C properties: mRadioactiveDecay: 0 - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/NuclearWaste/Desc_NuclearWaste.Desc_NuclearWaste_C properties: mRadioactiveDecay: 0 Repeat the patch entry for every radioactive descriptor you want to neutralise (uranium fuel rods, plutonium parts, …).

sections.heading: Conveyor belt speed: ALL belts at once
sections.text: Every belt mark derives from the native AFGBuildableConveyorBelt, so one subclass-expanded patch covers Mk.1 through Mk.6 (and modded belts!): type: cdo patches: - target: /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildableConveyorBelt applyToSubclasses: true # Mk.1–Mk.6 + every modded belt class properties: mSpeed: $op: multiply value: 2 > ℹ️ mSpeed is not items/min. It is stored in the engine's internal unit (cm/s scaled by 2), > so a Mk.1 belt's "60 items/min" is not 60 here. Prefer relative ops (multiply) over absolute > set values, and verify the resulting throughput in-game.

sections.heading: Schematics (`UFGSchematic`)
sections.text: UFGSchematic backs every unlockable in the game: HUB milestones, MAM research nodes, and AWESOME Shop entries alike. It's the single class to patch whether you're rebalancing progression cost, research time, or which tier something unlocks at. The properties in play are mType, mDisplayName, mDescription, mSchematicCategory, mSubCategories, mMenuPriority, mTechTier, mCost, mTimeToComplete, mUnlocks, mSchematicIcon, mSmallSchematicIcon, mSchematicDependencies, mHiddenUntilDependenciesMet, and mRelevantEvents. The patch below shrinks a tutorial schematic's completion time to a tenth, clears its cost array so it's free, and clamps its tech tier into the valid range from 0 to 9: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Tutorial/Schematic_Tutorial1.Schematic_Tutorial1_C properties: mTimeToComplete: $op: multiply value: 0.1 mCost: $op: clear # free! mTechTier: $op: clamp min: 0 max: 9

sections.heading: Making a milestone free
sections.text: Same mechanism, applied to a HUB milestone: clear the cost array and set the cooldown to (nearly) nothing: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-1.Schematic_1-1_C properties: mCost: $op: clear # no item cost mTimeToComplete: 1 # 1-second freighter turnaround

sections.heading: Research / M.A.M. (`UFGResearchTree`)
sections.text: M.A.M. research trees are their own class, UFGResearchTree, separate from the schematic nodes they unlock. This class supplies the tree's own display name and grouping in the M.A.M. menu. Renaming a tree, for a total-conversion pack or just to fix a typo, is a one-line patch against that display name: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Research/Mycelia_RS/ResearchTree_Mycelia.ResearchTree_Mycelia_C properties: mDisplayName: 'Mycelia (Rebalanced)'

sections.heading: Categories (`UFGItemCategory`, `UFGSchematicCategory`)
sections.text: Categories are the group headers shown above rows of items in the inventory and build menus, and above schematic groups in the M.A.M. and AWESOME Shop. They hold nothing but display metadata, so renaming one is the same mDisplayName patch as any other descriptor. Just target the category asset instead of an item or schematic: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/ItemCategories/Cat_Ingots.Cat_Ingots_C properties: mDisplayName: 'Metals'

sections.heading: Vehicles (`AFGWheeledVehicle`)
sections.text: UFGVehicleDescriptor (the buildable-menu entry) only points at the actual vehicle class, the tunable stats live on AFGWheeledVehicle itself, same as any other actor CDO: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Vehicle/Tractor/BP_Tractor.BP_Tractor_C properties: mManualFuelConsumption: $op: multiply value: 0.75 # 25% less fuel while driven manually mAutopilotFuelConsumption: $op: multiply value: 0.75 mInventorySize: 12 applyToSubclasses: true on /Script/FactoryGame.FGWheeledVehicle tunes every vehicle (Tractor, Truck, Explorer, Cyber Wagon, and modded vehicles) in one patch, same as the belt-speed example above.

sections.heading: Trains (`AFGLocomotive`)
sections.text: The locomotive's power draw is an FFloatInterval (idle/full-throttle range), not a flat number: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Vehicle/Train/Locomotive/BP_Locomotive.BP_Locomotive_C properties: mPowerConsumption: Min: 5 Max: 80 # MW; vanilla is roughly Min 15 and Max 110 There's no separate top-level "max speed" stat on the locomotive to patch, speed on a given track segment is governed by curvature/signals, not a flat per-locomotive cap.

sections.heading: Creatures (`AFGCreature`, `AFGCreatureDescriptor`)
sections.text: Creature identity/UI lives on the lightweight UFGCreatureDescriptor (mostly just a pointer at the creature class plus arachnophobia-mode icons); combat/movement stats live on AFGCreature itself and its movement data, reflectable the same way. Move speed is a lookup table (mMoveSpeedData: TArray<FMoveSpeedPair>, one entry per EMoveSpeed, MS_Walk/MS_Run/ MS_Sprint), so target the entry by index rather than a single flat property: type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Character/Creature/Stinger/Char_Stinger.Char_Stinger_C properties: # index 2 = MS_Sprint in the base game's authored order mMoveSpeedData[2].Speed: $op: multiply value: 0.75 # 25% slower at a sprint > ℹ️ Array index isn't guaranteed by the enum value, confirm which index holds which > MoveSpeedType for your target creature (export it from the in-game editor, or check > /kdf report after a dry patch) rather than assuming index order matches EMoveSpeed's > declaration order. > ⚠️ Spawner density fields are per-instance, not a class default. AFGCreatureSpawner > (mNumberOfCreatures, mCanSpawnDuringDay/mCanSpawnDuringNight, mRespawnTimeIndays) controls > _how many_ creatures a given spawner produces, but every spawner is a pre-placed level actor, > its property values are baked into the map/save data at placement time, the same way an > already-built building keeps its saved values after a CDO edit (see > Power & Machines → Runtime actor patches). > A cdo patch to AFGCreatureSpawner changes the class default, which only affects spawners > that don't already have their own saved override, in practice, treat this as unverified until > you've confirmed it in-game on your target save, and prefer patching the creature class itself > (as above) for stats that are meant to apply uniformly.

sections.heading: Bulk edits with the tag matcher
sections.text: Patching one target at a time doesn't scale once you want "every alternate recipe" or "every Tier 3+ schematic" to shift together. matchTag (with a required ofClass scope) finds every CDO or asset of that class, including subclasses, that carries the given gameplay tag, then applies the same ops to all of them in one patch entry. The tag container property is auto-detected, but it can be pinned explicitly with tagProperty when a class exposes more than one. The example below speeds up every recipe carrying the KMods.AlternateRecipe tag by 20%: type: cdo patches: - matchTag: KMods.AlternateRecipe # every recipe carrying this tag … ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe tagProperty: mGameplayTags properties: # … gets 20% faster mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.8

sections.heading: Buffing all alternate recipes (KAPI tags)
sections.text: KMods.AlternateRecipe is a KAPI-registered native tag, so gate the document behind hasMod. Without KAPI, the tag does not exist and the document is skipped with an Info diagnostic: type: cdo conditions: hasMod: KAPI patches: - matchTag: KMods.AlternateRecipe ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.75 # all alternates 25% faster mVariablePowerConsumptionFactor: $op: multiply value: 0.9 Registering and matching your own tags works the same way. See Game Tags.

sections.heading: Bulk edits by producer building (`producedIn`)
sections.text: Not everything you want to select carries a tag. The most common recipe question is "everything crafted in machine X", and producedIn: answers it directly. It defaults its scope to FGRecipe, takes one class or a list, and a recipe matches when its mProducedIn references that class **or a subclass of it**. Full class paths, bare class names, and generated-content ids all work: type: cdo patches: # every Constructor recipe: 25% faster - producedIn: Build_ConstructorMk1_C properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.75 # every Assembler OR Manufacturer recipe: 10% less power (variable-power recipes) - producedIn: - /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/AssemblerMk1/Build_AssemblerMk1.Build_AssemblerMk1_C - /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/ManufacturerMk1/Build_ManufacturerMk1.Build_ManufacturerMk1_C properties: mVariablePowerConsumptionFactor: $op: multiply value: 0.9 The subclass rule turns the native base classes into families. Three are worth memorising: | producedIn: value | Selects every recipe crafted … | | /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildableManufacturer | in any manufacturing machine: Constructor, Assembler, Manufacturer, Refinery, Blender, Packager, … and modded machines built on the same base | | /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildGun | with the build gun, that is every buildable's build recipe | | /Script/FactoryGame.FGWorkBench | by hand at the Craft Bench / Equipment Workshop (BP_WorkBenchComponent_C and friends derive from it) | type: cdo patches: # hand-crafting is twice as fast, everywhere - producedIn: /Script/FactoryGame.FGWorkBench properties: mManualManufacturingMultiplier: $op: multiply value: 0.5 # every buildable costs 20% less (rounded down by the game per ingredient) - producedIn: /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildGun where: path: mIngredients isEmpty: false properties: mIngredients[0].Amount: $op: multiply value: 0.8

sections.heading: Bulk edits by ingredient or product
sections.text: ingredient: and product: follow the same rules for mIngredients and mProduct: an item class (or a base class, to catch every item deriving from it), one or many, any-of. They stack with each other and with producedIn:; every filter on the entry has to hold: type: cdo patches: # everything that consumes Plastic or Rubber crafts 10% faster - ingredient: - Desc_Plastic_C - Desc_Rubber_C properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.9 # every recipe producing Screws in an Assembler yields double - product: Desc_IronScrew_C producedIn: Build_AssemblerMk1_C properties: mProduct[0].Amount: $op: multiply value: 2 # every recipe that produces ANY equipment (subclass rule on an item base class) - product: /Script/FactoryGame.FGEquipmentDescriptor properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.5 mProduct[0].Amount addresses the first product. For recipes with several outputs, use update_where when the position is unknown: - product: Desc_IronScrew_C properties: mProduct: $op: update_where where: path: ItemClass equals: Desc_IronScrew_C value: Amount: 24 The outer product: selects recipes. The operation's where: independently selects matching elements inside each recipe's mProduct array.

sections.heading: Bulk edits by name pattern (`matchName`)
sections.text: Vanilla content follows naming conventions, and matchName: lets you select on them without tags. Patterns are case-insensitive wildcards; the _C suffix is optional, and a pattern containing / is matched against the full class path so you can select by content folder: type: cdo patches: # every vanilla alternate recipe, no KAPI dependency needed - ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe matchName: Recipe_Alternate_* properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.8 # every milestone (Progression folder) researches twice as fast - ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGSchematic matchName: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/* properties: mTimeToComplete: $op: multiply value: 0.5

sections.heading: Bulk edits by property value (`where`)
sections.text: where: compares any reflected property of every candidate in an ofClass: scope. One map, or a list of maps using AND by default. Add sibling whereMode: OR when any clause may hold. Each map has a path: and exactly one operator (equals, notEquals, lessThan, lessOrEqual, greaterThan, greaterOrEqual, contains, notContains, matches, isEmpty). [*] in a path means "any element": type: cdo patches: # slow recipes (longer than 8 s) that use Iron Ingot get a bit faster - ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe where: - path: mManufactoringDuration greaterThan: 8 - path: mIngredients[*].ItemClass equals: Desc_IronIngot_C properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.8 # every schematic up to tier 3 unlocks instantly - ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGSchematic where: path: mTechTier lessOrEqual: 3 properties: mTimeToComplete: 0 # every liquid or gas: no sink points (`in` = any of the listed values; enums compare by name) - ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGItemDescriptor where: path: mForm in: - RF_LIQUID - RF_GAS properties: mResourceSinkPoints: 0 # items whose display name mentions "Nuclear" cannot be discarded - ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGItemDescriptor where: path: mDisplayName matches: "*Nuclear*" properties: mCanBeDiscarded: false # recipes with no producer at all become hand-craftable - ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe where: path: mProducedIn isEmpty: true properties: mProducedIn: $op: append value: /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/-Shared/WorkBench/BP_WorkBenchComponent.BP_WorkBenchComponent_C Reference-typed comparisons (equals/contains/in on a class or soft-class property) match the class or any subclass, the same way producedIn: does, so path: mProducedIn / `contains: /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildableManufacturer is the long-hand spelling of producedIn:`, and path: mProducedIn with an in list containing Constructor and Assembler is the long-hand form of a two-entry producedIn: list. The full operator table lives on Targeting.

sections.heading: Removing content in bulk
sections.text: The same filters drive remove:. Taking every Particle Accelerator recipe and every tier-8 milestone out of the game is two short documents; the mechanics, save impact, and the recipe-plus-schematic pairing are on Removing Content: type: recipe remove: - producedIn: Build_HadronCollider_C type: schematic remove: - where: path: mTechTier greaterOrEqual: 8

pages.title: A complete building
pages.description: Create a building, its build and production recipes, schematic, and sink points in dependency order within one pack.

sections.heading: A complete building
sections.text: This example builds the full reference chain for dynamic content in dependency order. All copy-pasteable YAML belongs to one pack: # file: pack.yml ref: MyFactory name: My Factory Pack version: 1.0.0 Every step references the previous one by generated class path. The id: of each entry is the contract that makes those paths deterministic, in the form /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_<Id> (see YAML Schema → generated class identity). :::caution[Honest scope callout, read this first] A truly new machine with its own mesh or its own logic is out of scope. KDataForge is 2D-only (no mesh import, ever) and generated classes copy their parent's layout (no new components or reflected properties). This chain **re-skins and re-parametrises existing buildable behaviour**: your machine looks like and ticks like its parent, but is a separate class with its own build-menu entry, recipes, stats, and save identity. For genuinely new behaviour you need real C++/Blueprint content. :::

sections.heading: The ordering guarantee
sections.text: You never need include: between these files. Stages run in a fixed order. The whole Items stage, which generates buildables via class, descriptors via building, and items via item, finishes before Recipes starts. Recipes in turn finishes before Schematics starts. Within Items, the generation types are priority-ordered. So every file below can reference every class generated in an earlier step by its /KDataForge/Gen/... path, regardless of file names or scan order.

sections.heading: Step 1: the buildable actor (`type: class`)
sections.text: Does type: building create the building actor? No, type: building generates the _descriptor_, which is the build-menu entry. The buildable actor, the Build_X_C class placed in the world, generally comes from an existing buildable parent. You define a type: class entry with parent: set to an existing /Game/....Build_*_C, effectively reparenting an existing buildable. There are no custom meshes, since the policy is 2D-only, and no new components. You get the parent's mesh, connections, and production logic, with your own CDO overrides. # file: 1-buildable.class.yml type: class classes: - id: Build_MyMachine parent: /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/SmelterMk1/Build_SmelterMk1.Build_SmelterMk1_C properties: mDisplayName: key: Build_MyMachine_Name ns: MyFactory source: Compact Smelter mPowerConsumption: 12.0 This generates /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Build_MyMachine, a real AFGBuildableManufacturer subclass via the smelter parent.

sections.heading: Step 2: the building descriptor (`type: building`)
sections.text: The FGBuildingDescriptor subclass whose mBuildableClass points at the buildable from step 1: # file: 2-descriptor.building.yml type: building buildings: - id: Desc_MyMachine properties: mDisplayName: key: Desc_MyMachine_Name ns: MyFactory source: Compact Smelter mBuildableClass: /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Build_MyMachine See Buildings for the descriptor-vs-buildable split in general.

sections.heading: Step 3: the build recipe (`type: recipe`)
sections.text: Construction recipes are ordinary FGRecipes whose product is the building descriptor. Their mProducedIn includes the build gun, which is how the game knows a recipe belongs in the build menu: # file: 3-build-recipe.recipe.yml type: recipe recipes: - id: Recipe_Build_MyMachine properties: mDisplayName: Compact Smelter mIngredients: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronPlateReinforced/Desc_IronPlateReinforced.Desc_IronPlateReinforced_C Amount: 4 - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/Rotor/Desc_Rotor.Desc_Rotor_C Amount: 2 mProduct: - ItemClass: /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Desc_MyMachine Amount: 1 mProducedIn: - /Script/FactoryGame.FGBuildGun

sections.heading: Step 4: production recipes for the machine (`type: recipe`)
sections.text: This step defines what the machine can produce: recipes whose mProducedIn is the **generated buildable class** from step 1. Adding a new item for it to produce shows the item side of the chain too: # file: 4a-output-item.item.yml type: item items: - id: Desc_CompactIngot parent: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties: mDisplayName: key: Desc_CompactIngot_Name ns: MyFactory source: Compact Ingot mStackSize: SS_HUGE :::note[Stack-size caveat] The engine caches item stack sizes. KDataForge automatically resets the descriptor's cached stack size (mCachedStackSize) whenever an op writes mStackSize, so the value above just works. Inventories that already contain the item may need the item re-added (or a game reload) to reflect a changed limit. Details: YAML Schema → Special-cased properties. ::: # file: 4b-production-recipe.recipe.yml type: recipe recipes: - id: Recipe_CompactIngot properties: mDisplayName: Compact Ingot mIngredients: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/OreIron/Desc_OreIron.Desc_OreIron_C Amount: 2 mProduct: - ItemClass: /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Desc_CompactIngot Amount: 1 mManufactoringDuration: 3.0 mProducedIn: - /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Build_MyMachine # the step-1 buildable

sections.heading: Step 5: the schematic (`type: schematic`)
sections.text: Unlocks both recipes via an instanced FGUnlockRecipe: # file: 5-schematic.schematic.yml type: schematic schematics: - id: Schematic_MyMachine properties: mDisplayName: Compact Smelting mType: EST_Milestone mTechTier: 2 mCost: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronPlate/Desc_IronPlate.Desc_IronPlate_C Amount: 100 unlocks: - class: /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties: mRecipes: - /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Recipe_Build_MyMachine - /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Recipe_CompactIngot Registering the schematic auto-propagates: its recipes register, and the recipes' items register in turn. The schematic is therefore the only piece you strictly need register: for (see Recipes → auto-propagation).

sections.heading: Step 6: sinkpoints for the new items (`type: sinkpoints`)
sections.text: New items have no AWESOME Sink value until you give them one: # file: 6-sinkpoints.sinkpoints.yml type: sinkpoints track: Default entries: - item: /KDataForge/Gen/MyFactory.Gen_MyFactory_Desc_CompactIngot points: 8

sections.heading: Recap: the chain at a glance
sections.text: Six files, six generation steps, each one consuming the class path the previous one produced. The table below is a quick lookup for which file generates what and what it points back at, once you have read the walkthrough above: | # | File | Generates | References | | 1 | 1-buildable.class.yml | buildable actor class | existing Build_SmelterMk1_C parent | | 2 | 2-descriptor.building.yml | building descriptor | step 1 via mBuildableClass | | 3 | 3-build-recipe.recipe.yml | build recipe | step 2 as mProduct, FGBuildGun in mProducedIn | | 4 | 4a/4b | output item + production recipe | step 1 in mProducedIn, item in mProduct | | 5 | 5-schematic.schematic.yml | schematic | steps 3+4 via FGUnlockRecipe | | 6: Session restart | Did you restart after editing generated content? | /kdf reload rescans YAML, but frozen content registrations and cold changes still need a new session | Ids are the contract. You can rename any file freely, but renaming an id needs a redirects: entry in pack.yml (see Conditions & Packs). Custom Classes explains the generic generation escape hatch used in step 1. The Buildings, Recipes, Schematics, and Sink Points pages cover each later capability. Use the content-creation schema for exact fields. End-to-End Pack is the item-centric counterpart to this building walkthrough.

pages.title: Delivery task trees
pages.description: Build a five-node UKAPIDeliveryTask tree with every node property, negative coordinates, multi-flag mParentTask values, the full Endless field set, completion-based tree unlocks, and a schematic force-unlock.

sections.heading: Delivery task trees
sections.text: UKAPIDeliveryTask is KAPI's 2D research-tree node type: a small reward/task, placed on an integer coordinate grid, that unlocks once its neighboring parent node(s) are completed. This feature has no Satisfactory Plus dependency it only needs KAPI + KPrivateCodeLib, so it's usable from any mod that links those two. The example builds one complete tree from start to finish. For every other KAPI data asset type, see Adding KAPI Data Assets; for the underlying YAML grammar mParentTask uses, see Value Forms.

sections.heading: The grid and `mParentTask`
sections.text: Each node has an mCoordinate (FIntVector2 with X and Y fields; negative values are perfectly valid, the grid isn't anchored to the origin) and an mParentTask bitmask using EKAPIDeliveryTaskParent. Each flag maps to a bit and fixed coordinate offset **relative to the node itself**: | Flag | Mask | Parent is at | | None | 0 | no parent | | Above | 1 | (X, Y - 1) | | Left | 2 | (X - 1, Y) | | Right | 4 | (X + 1, Y) | | Bottom | 8 | (X, Y + 1) | | AboveLeft | 16 | (X - 1, Y - 1) | | AboveRight | 32 | (X + 1, Y - 1) | | BelowLeft | 64 | (X - 1, Y + 1) | | BelowRight | 128 | (X + 1, Y + 1) | Every flag set on a node must point at a coordinate some other node in the tree actually occupies, or the node is rejected at load time. Use one flag name for one parent and a YAML sequence for multiple parents. When property metadata and the loaded enum are available under WITH_METADATA, KDataForge resolves and ORs scalar names, sequences, and |-joined strings ("Above|Left"). EKAPIDeliveryTaskParent declares mask values, so Above (1) and Left (2) combine to 3. Raw integer masks such as 3 are accepted by set only; append/prepend and remove require names. If property metadata is stripped or the enum cannot be resolved, this integer property uses ordinary numeric conversion; named bitmask forms and mutations are unavailable. Shipping builds must retain metadata for these named examples. See Property Types for mask-value versus bit-index rules and width limits. mRequiredParentCompletions defaults to 1 and raises the completed-run threshold for every marked parent. This is useful behind an endless parent: mParentTask: Bottom mRequiredParentCompletions: 10 Values below 1 are rejected. A queued parent can satisfy default one-run topology so its child can be placed later in same queue. Thresholds above 1 count completed runs only; queued repeats do not unlock or pre-queue child.

sections.heading: Supporting assets
sections.text: The tree below sets every applicable property on every node, including the icon, ADA message, and Endless-only amount-multiplier curve those fields reference. Those three are generated by a small support file, include:-ed so they load first (dataasset/curve/asset all run in the same Assets stage, so ordering across document types is otherwise just file order, not implicit see Document Structure): # file: showcase-delivery-task-support.yml type: asset assets: - id: DeliveryTaskIcon file: mod-logo.png # pack-relative path any 2D image works as a placeholder --- type: dataasset conditions: hasMod: KAPI assets: - id: AdaMessage_TaskComplete class: /Script/FactoryGame.FGMessage # UFGMessage is a UPrimaryDataAsset, so `dataasset` builds it directly properties: mTitle: "Delivery Complete" mMessage: "Another delivery task in the showcase tree has been completed." --- type: curve curveType: float curves: - id: DeliveryTaskAmountMultiplier defaultValue: 1 preInfinityExtrap: constant postInfinityExtrap: linear isEventCurve: false keys: - time: 0 value: 1 interpMode: linear - time: 5 value: 2.5 interpMode: linear

sections.heading: A complete five-node tree
sections.text: This tree deliberately starts off-origin, in negative coordinate space, to show the grid isn't restricted to (0, 0)-anchored positive layouts. Every node sets every UKAPIDataAssetBase common field (mName/mDescription/mIcon/mIsDisabled/mPriority/mTags) and every UKAPIDeliveryTask field common to both variants (mAdaMessages/mToastIcon/mToastText). DeliveryTask_Right is switched to bIsEndless: true to demonstrate the complete Endless-only field set (mPoolElements/mTaskRewards/mMaxTasks/mAmountMultiplierCurve/ mAbsolutMaxItemAmount) that a One-Time node never sets; every other node stays One-Time (bIsEndless: false) and sets the complete One-Time field set (mRewards/mCosts, plus mSchematics on the last node): # file: showcase-delivery-task.dataasset.yml type: dataasset conditions: hasMod: KAPI include: - showcase-delivery-task-support.yml assets: - id: DeliveryTask_Root class: /Script/KAPI.KAPIDeliveryTask properties: # --- UKAPIDataAssetBase common fields --- mName: "Root Task" mDescription: "The starting node of the showcase tree. No parent required." mIcon: DeliveryTaskIcon mIsDisabled: false mPriority: 0 mTags: - KMods.EventOnly # --- UKAPIDeliveryTask common fields --- mAdaMessages: - AdaMessage_TaskComplete mToastIcon: DeliveryTaskIcon mToastText: "You completed the Root Task." mCoordinate: X: -2 Y: -1 # mParentTask / bRequireAllParents intentionally omitted the root has no parent, and # bRequireAllParents is ignored once there's nothing to require. bIsEndless: false # --- One-Time fields (bIsEndless: false) --- mRewards: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C Amount: 50 # mCosts omitted empty cost list makes this tree entry free. - id: DeliveryTask_Above class: /Script/KAPI.KAPIDeliveryTask properties: mName: "Single-Parent Child" mDescription: "Requires only the Above parent (Root)." mIcon: DeliveryTaskIcon mIsDisabled: false mPriority: 0 mTags: - KMods.EventOnly mAdaMessages: - AdaMessage_TaskComplete mToastIcon: DeliveryTaskIcon mToastText: "You completed the Single-Parent Child task." mCoordinate: X: -2 Y: 0 # Above -> (-2, -1): Root mParentTask: Above bRequireAllParents: true bIsEndless: false mRewards: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronPlate/Desc_IronPlate.Desc_IronPlate_C Amount: 50 mCosts: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C Amount: 20 - id: DeliveryTask_Right class: /Script/KAPI.KAPIDeliveryTask properties: mName: "Endless Sibling Child" mDescription: "Requires only the Left parent (Root). Endless variant demonstrates every Endless field." mIcon: DeliveryTaskIcon mIsDisabled: false mPriority: 0 mTags: - KMods.EventOnly mAdaMessages: - AdaMessage_TaskComplete mToastIcon: DeliveryTaskIcon mToastText: "You completed another round of the Endless Sibling Child task." mCoordinate: X: -1 Y: -1 # Left -> (-2, -1): Root mParentTask: Left bRequireAllParents: true bIsEndless: true # --- Endless-only fields (bIsEndless: true) --- mPoolElements: - mItem: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C mAmountRange: LowerBound: Type: Inclusive Value: 50 UpperBound: Type: Exclusive Value: 200 mRequiredTas: -1 # INDEX_NONE eligible from the very first roll mTaskRewards: - mRewards: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronPlate/Desc_IronPlate.Desc_IronPlate_C Amount: 25 mRequiredTask: -1 # INDEX_NONE granted on every completion mMaxTasks: 10 # INDEX_NONE/-1 would mean uncapped concurrent slots mAmountMultiplierCurve: DeliveryTaskAmountMultiplier mAbsolutMaxItemAmount: RF_SOLID: DeliveryTaskAmountMultiplier RF_LIQUID: DeliveryTaskAmountMultiplier -
