This asset governs how much: production per hit, a hit cap, the trace range used to scan for valid targets, and min/max output bounds around a base count. clamp is the natural op for a range-scan property like mRangeToScan, since it lets you pin the value inside sane bounds in one step instead of chaining min/max: type: cdo conditions: hasMod: KAPI patches: - allAssetsOfClass: /Script/KAPI.KAPIAirCollectorData properties: mProduceItemCountMax: $op: add value: 2 mRangeToScan: $op: clamp min: 1000 max: 50000 Other properties: mItemClass, mActorClass, mProductionTime, mProductionPerHit, mMaxHit, mTraceChannel, mRecipePrio, mProduceItemCountBase, mProduceItemCountMin.

sections.heading: `UKAPIManufacturerModifications`: manufacturer I/O tuning
sections.text: Rather than editing every recipe a manufacturer building runs, this asset lets you scale an entire building class's throughput at once. Solid, fluid, and gas connections each get their own multiplier, plus there are separate slot-icon overrides for solid and fluid connectors. It's the tool of choice when the goal is "every recipe on this building runs faster/slower" instead of "this one recipe": type: cdo conditions: hasMod: KAPI patches: - allAssetsOfClass: /Script/KAPI.KAPIManufacturerModifications properties: mSolidMultiplier: $op: multiply value: 2 Other properties: mTargetClass, mInput, mOutput, mFluidMultiplier, mGasMultiplier, mSolidSlotIcons, mFluidSlotIcons.

sections.heading: `UKAPISugHatchingData`: slug breeding/hatching
sections.text: This is the largest KAPI data asset type by property count, since it drives a full breeding-simulation mechanic. It covers which slug and egg pair it describes, breeding/hatching/die durations, the environmental comfort window (heat, humidity, compatible neighbors) the pair needs, food and fluid/power consumption rates, incubator/tank tier requirements, and the output counts and odds for the resulting eggs or slugs. Breeding time and hatch chance are the two levers most packs touch first: type: cdo conditions: hasMod: KAPI patches: - allAssetsOfClass: /Script/KAPI.KAPISugHatchingData properties: mBreedingTime: $op: multiply value: 0.5 mChance: $op: max value: 0.1 The full property set: mSlug, mEgg, mEggColor, mSlugTier, mChance, mProbability, mHatchDuration, mDieTime, mDayTime, mMinHeat/mMaxHeat, mMinHumidity/mMaxHumidity, mComfortableWith, mRequiredFood, mFoodConsumePerCycle, mFoodDuration, mFluidClass, mFluidConsume, mFluidConsumeTime, mPowerConsume, mIncubatorTier, mTankTier, mProductionCount, mProductionCountEggs, mFixedChanceMultiplier, mPossibleSlugs.

sections.heading: `UKAPIExtractorAllowList`: scanner/extractor allow lists
sections.text: Rather than a per-resource property, this asset is a compatibility table: which resource types a given extractor building is allowed (or explicitly disallowed) to mine, and the mirror image of which extractors a given resource accepts. That makes it the right place to hook up a new resource type, or a new miner added by another mod, so they recognize each other. Do this by appending to the relevant list instead of replacing it wholesale: type: cdo conditions: hasMod: KAPI patches: - allAssetsOfClass: /Script/KAPI.KAPIExtractorAllowList properties: mAllowedExtractors: $op: append value: - /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/MinerMk3/Build_MinerMk3.Build_MinerMk3_C Other properties: mAllowedResources, mDisallowResources, mDisallowExtractors.

sections.heading: `UKAPTooltipWidgetInjector`: tooltip widget injection
sections.text: This one doesn't tune gameplay numbers at all. It injects an extra UI widget into item tooltips for a filtered set of classes, at a chosen position in the tooltip's widget list. mWidgetClass is the key field here (the widget that actually gets inserted), so it carries the same never-null guarantee as mResourceClass and mInFluid.ItemClass above: type: cdo conditions: hasMod: KAPI patches: - allAssetsOfClass: /Script/KAPI.KAPTooltipWidgetInjector properties: mInjectAtIndex: 0 Other properties: mClassFilter.

sections.heading: `FKDFRandomData` note & key-field warning
sections.text: FKAPIRandomData (with its mProbability field) appears nested inside several of the asset types above rather than as its own top-level asset. Edit it the same way as any other nested struct member, through a dotted path like mSomething.mProbability. > ⚠️ KAPI crashes intentionally (fgcheck) when a key field is null: mResourceClass on miner > descriptions, mInFluid.ItemClass on cleaner items, mWidgetClass on tooltip injectors. Never > set these to none. Use mIsDisabled: true to turn an asset off instead.

sections.heading: KMods native gameplay tags
sections.text: KAPI registers a handful of gameplay tags itself at startup, so they're usable in matchTag: (and in any tag-container op) immediately, without your pack needing its own gametag document first. These are KMods.ExcludeFromNodeRandomization, KMods.Disabled, KMods.AlternateRecipe, KMods.PlannerExclude, KMods.WikiExclude, KMods.Deprecated, KMods.WIP, KMods.Cheat, and KMods.EventOnly. Since mTags lives on the common UKAPIDataAssetBase, any of them works as a matchTag: selector across every KAPI asset type shown above, not just the one it was originally meant for: type: cdo conditions: hasMod: KAPI patches: - matchTag: KMods.Cheat # hide all cheat-tagged KAPI content ofClass: /Script/KAPI.KAPIDataAssetBase properties: mIsDisabled: true See Game Tags for how matchTag: and tag-container ops work in general, and Tag-Based Bulk Balancing for a full worked example built around this exact tag list.

sections.heading: Creating new instances: `type: dataasset`
sections.text: Editing only gets you so far. Sometimes a pack genuinely needs a new data asset instance that doesn't exist yet, such as a new modular miner resource, a new cleaner recipe, or a new slug pairing. A dataasset document creates a real UDataAsset instance at runtime in package /KDataForge/GenAssets/<PackRef> under a save-stable name Gen_<PackRef>_<Id>, and announces it to the asset registry. Primary-asset behavior still belongs to the chosen class; if the class derives from UPrimaryDataAsset, consumers that scan the registry for that asset type can pick the new instance up on their next scan: # file: cleaner.dataasset.yml type: dataasset conditions: hasMod: KAPI assets: - id: CleanerItem_MyFluid class: /Script/KAPI.KAPICleanerItemDescription # any UDataAsset subclass properties: mProductionTime: 4.0 mInFluid: ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/Water/Desc_Water.Desc_Water_C Amount: 1000 dataasset runs in the Assets stage, the second stage in the pipeline, right after GameTags and before Localization/CDOChanges. This means a generated instance already exists by the time any later cdo, item, or recipe document in the same load needs to reference it. YAML changes are loaded on the next session start. The same example appears inside the end-to-end pack in End-to-End Pack. There it sits next to the item/recipe/schematic files it belongs with. Remember: dataasset is only for creating new instances. Existing data assets, whether UPrimaryDataAsset or plain UDataAsset, are already editable via the cdo selectors shown above. There's no need to "recreate" one just to change a value on it.

sections.heading: Generated ADA messages and automatic triggers
sections.text: Generated /Script/FactoryGame.FGMessage data assets join the host/server's native Story message list when the gameplay world starts. Their existing mTrigger and mConditions properties use normal game event handling, including schematic-purchase triggers. No additional event-rule or manual playback binding is required for a schematic-triggered message. Only successfully configured, active, non-legacy messages are included. Files ending in .yml.disabled remain inactive. KDF.Reload reconciles active generated messages without adding duplicates or resetting played-message history. Removing a definition removes its automatic trigger registration; previously played messages remain in history. Triggers react to new events: loading a save with an already purchased milestone does not replay its message. Keep message IDs stable to preserve normal once-only playback. To diagnose discovery, check the Story message synchronization log entry and use getall FGStorySubsystem mAllMessages in the game console. Verify playback with a fresh purchase of the target schematic.

sections.heading: 2D image assets: `type: asset`
sections.text: Generated items and buildings need icons, and those icons have to come from somewhere. Your pack doesn't ship a .uasset, it ships a plain image file instead. An asset document loads an image file shipped inside your pack and turns it into a real, referenceable UTexture2D. This is the missing piece for giving generated content its own icon instead of borrowing one from an existing item: <your-mod>/DataForge/ pack.yml # ref: MyPack icons/ my-icon.png my-icons.asset.yml # file: my-icons.asset.yml type: asset assets: - id: MyIcon file: icons/my-icon.png # relative to the pack root; png / jpg / tga / bmp The result is a transient UTexture2D at /KDataForge/GenAssets/<PackRef>.Gen_<PackRef>_<Id>, announced to the asset registry the same way a dataasset instance is: - Image changes are decoded on the next session start. - file: is pack-relative. Absolute paths and .. traversal outside the pack are rejected. - The texture object stays stable for the running GameInstance. A new session recreates the transient object and resolves YAML references again. - 2D only: no FBX/glTF, ever (design policy). Only PNG, JPG/JPEG, TGA, and BMP are decoded today. DDS and WAV aren't supported yet, and an unrecognized extension fails validation with the supported-format list in the error message.

sections.heading: Using a loaded image as an item icon
sections.text: Point any object-reference icon property, most commonly an item descriptor's mSmallIcon / mPersistentBigIcon, at the generated texture's path, exactly like referencing any other asset: type: cdo patches: - target: MySuperIngot # a generated item short id, same as /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_MySuperIngot # …or any existing one: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties: mSmallIcon: MyIcon # short id same as /KDataForge/GenAssets/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_MyIcon mPersistentBigIcon: MyIcon Both target: and the icon values above use the bare id: because everything referenced was generated by this same pack. See Generated Content Short Ids for cross-pack resolution and the full path form. For a generated item you can just as well put these two entries straight into the item document's properties: instead (see Items), same ops, one file less.

sections.heading: Automatic consumer rescans
sections.text: Neither KAPI nor RRDA notice a new or changed data asset on their own. Somebody has to tell their scanning subsystem to look again, and KDataForge does that for you. After the initial load, it checks whether any data assets were modified or added and only then triggers a rescan. You never have to poke a subsystem yourself: - KAPI: rescanned via reflection only when the KAPI mod is actually loaded, no hard dependency needed. - RefinedRDApi: rescanned only when the RefinedRDApi mod is actually loaded, with no link dependency needed on it. It's what covers RefinedPower / FicsitFarming boiler/cooler/heater/turbine/generator/dirt data assets, below.

sections.heading: Editing RefinedR&D data assets (RRDA)
sections.text: RefinedPower and FicsitFarming machine tuning lives in the same kind of PrimaryDataAsset instance KAPI uses, just under RRDA's own classes: RRDABoilerDataAsset, RRDACoolerDataAsset, RRDAHeaterDataAsset, RRDATurbineDataAsset, RRDAGeneratorDataAsset, and RRDADirtDataAsset. All of these are editable with plain cdo documents exactly like the KAPI types above. Because the rescan that picks up your changes runs entirely via reflection (see above), a hasMod condition is all the gating a pack needs. There's no RRDA API dependency to add: # file: faster-boilers.cdo.yml type: cdo conditions: hasMod: RefinedRDApi patches: - allAssetsOfClass: /Script/RefinedRDApi.RRDABoilerDataAsset properties: mDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.5 # every RefinedPower/FicsitFarming boiler produces twice as fast Heater and turbine assets work identically: swap the class (allAssetsOfClass: /Script/RefinedRDApi.RRDAHeaterDataAsset, …RRDATurbineDataAsset) and patch their properties the same way. /kdf report lists every matched asset so you can confirm the selection before tuning values. See Editing Another Mod's Data Assets for a full walkthrough that starts from "I don't know this mod's class names yet" and ends with a working balance pack.

pages.title: Event rules
pages.description: Run bounded server-side actions at world start or after a schematic purchase, optionally once per save.

sections.heading: Event rules
sections.text: Use type: eventrule to connect a gameplay event to a schematic grant or a diagnostic log entry. Rules run on the host or dedicated server. Clients do not execute the actions independently; schematic changes use the game's existing unlock and replication path.

sections.heading: First rule
sections.text: Place this document in a pack YAML file: type: eventrule rules: - id: world-start-log event: worldReady actions: - log: Factory rules are active in this save. The message appears in the game log once for this pack and save. It does not create a toast or player-facing message. log is diagnostic text, not localized UI text.

sections.heading: React to a schematic purchase
sections.text: type: eventrule rules: - id: progression-followup event: schematicPurchased schematic: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-1.Schematic_1-1_C actions: - unlockSchematic: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_2-3.Schematic_2-3_C - log: Follow-up schematic granted. Replace the class references with schematics appropriate for your progression. unlockSchematic grants access without paying its material cost; choose this action only for an intended reward. The game must allow the grant when the event occurs. This rule does not bypass a mod's CanGiveAccessToSchematic restrictions. An already purchased schematic is a successful no-op. The schematic filter is optional. Omitting it listens to every future schematic purchase. Schematics bought before the rules subscribed are not replayed. Use worldReady with requiresSchematics when you explicitly want to check progress already stored in a save.

sections.heading: Conditions and repetition
sections.text: type: eventrule rules: - id: log-existing-progress event: worldReady once: false requiresSchematics: - /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-1.Schematic_1-1_C actions: - log: Required progression is present at world start. Every requiresSchematics entry must already be purchased when the event is handled. The list is an AND condition; an empty or omitted list imposes no condition. A failed condition performs no actions and does not mark the rule completed. Conditions are evaluated at events, not every frame. once defaults to true: a successful rule's identity is stored in the save. Its identity is the pack ref plus rule id, compared without case. Reloading YAML, changing action contents, moving the document, or removing and later restoring the rule does not reset that history. Give an intentional new rule a new id. Keep a stable pack ref. With once: false, the rule may run again on later events. Within one originating event and all schematic purchases triggered by its actions, each matching rule is attempted at most once. This bounds feedback loops even for repeating rules. A dispatch cascade accepts at most 128 events; excess nested events are dropped with a warning.

sections.heading: Fields and limits
sections.text: | Field | Required | Meaning | | rules | Yes | Sequence of 1 to 256 rules per document. | | id | Yes | 1 to 128 ASCII letters, digits, ., _, or -; unique across the pack, ignoring case. | | event | Yes | Exactly worldReady or schematicPurchased. | | schematic | No | Schematic class filter; only valid with schematicPurchased. | | once | No | Boolean, default true. | | requiresSchematics | No | Sequence of up to 64 schematic class references. | | actions | Yes | Sequence of 1 to 32 actions. | Each action is a map containing exactly one key: unlockSchematic with a concrete schematic class, or log with nonblank text up to 2,048 characters. Unknown rule and action fields are errors. Field names and event names use the exact case shown above. Class references support the usual KDataForge class resolver, including generated content already created by earlier loader stages. The entire document is rejected if any rule is malformed, a class reference cannot resolve, or its rule IDs collide with rules already registered by another document. No actions run while loading or dry-running a document; validation and loading only register rules.

sections.heading: World lifecycle and reload
sections.text: worldReady fires after gameplay actors have begun play and the schematic manager is available. It is a world-load event. It does not fire again when YAML reload completes. Therefore a new worldReady rule added by live reload starts on the next world load. Updated purchase rules handle subsequent purchase events immediately after reload; earlier purchases are not replayed. On world travel or shutdown, subscriptions and pending events are removed. Once-per-save history belongs to the save, not the local configuration. On a client, these rules do not produce an independent reward or separate completion history. All schematic grants are checked before any action in a rule executes. If a grant cannot start, the rule logs a warning, executes no actions, and remains incomplete. If the game unexpectedly rejects a grant after the checks, earlier actions remain applied, later actions stop, and the rule remains incomplete. It may retry on a later matching event; already purchased grants are skipped. This is not an atomic rollback mechanism. Arrange dependent schematic grants as separate rules when the second grant only becomes valid after the first succeeds. The supported events are world start and schematic purchase. Delivery completion, arbitrary function calls, timers, continuous factory scans, and UI popups are not event-rule actions.

pages.title: Type: gametag
pages.description: Register gameplay tags at runtime and understand their syntax and load order.

sections.heading: Type: gametag
sections.text: A gametag document runs in the GameTags stage, which always runs first, before every other document type. The entries key for this document type is tags, given as a sequence. Changes are loaded on the next session start.

sections.heading: Minimal example
sections.text: A gametag document is a flat list of tag names to register. You can write each entry either as a bare string or as a map with an optional comment: for documentation purposes: # file: tags.gametag.yml type: gametag tags: - tag: MyOverhaul.Machines.Tier2 # map form with an optional comment comment: Marker for tier-2 machine rebalancing - MyOverhaul.Simple # scalar shorthand, no comment Each entry is either a plain tag-name string, or a map with tag: (required) and comment: (optional). The comment is purely documentation, shown in the tag picker/editor. The tag name itself must be a valid dot-separated gameplay tag string (Namespace.Category.Leaf...). Invalid strings are rejected at validation time, with the engine's own suggested fix included.

sections.heading: How registration actually works
sections.text: Registering a tag at runtime normally isn't possible: the engine's gameplay tag tree is built once at boot and isn't designed to be extended afterward. KDataForge works around this by adding the tag directly to the tag settings in memory and forcing a tree rebuild, entirely without touching any config file on disk. In practice, this gives you three consequences to keep in mind: - Tags exist only for the running session. They are not written to disk anywhere. Remove the YAML and the tag stops being registered on the _next_ boot. It is not retroactively unregistered from a session that already rebuilt the tree with it present. - Registration is idempotent: a tag already in GameplayTagList is skipped. - There is no tombstone or removal mechanism, unlike generated classes. Gameplay tags are cheap and additive, and the engine has no supported "unregister a tag" operation.

sections.heading: Ordering guarantee: use a tag the moment you register it
sections.text: The GameTags stage always runs before every other stage. This means a tag registered in one file is immediately available to matchTag: (and to mGameplayTags ops) in any cdo document in the same pack. No include: is needed for the gametag file itself. First, put the tag on some content: # file: tag-recipes.cdo.yml put the tag ON some content type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C properties: mGameplayTags: $op: append value: - MyOverhaul.Machines.Tier2 Then a second cdo document can select everything carrying that tag and patch it in bulk: # file: buff-tagged.cdo.yml match everything carrying the tag type: cdo include: - tag-recipes.cdo.yml # both files are in the CDOChanges stage order them explicitly patches: - matchTag: MyOverhaul.Machines.Tier2 ofClass: /Script/FactoryGame.FGRecipe tagProperty: mGameplayTags properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.8 tag-recipes.cdo.yml and buff-tagged.cdo.yml are both cdo documents, meaning both are in the CDOChanges stage. That is why _they_ need include: ordering between each other. The gametag document itself never needs it, since GameTags runs before CDOChanges unconditionally.

sections.heading: Tag container ops on `mGameplayTags`
sections.text: Once a tag exists, whether it is yours or a native KMods.* one (see Data Assets for the full native list), every tag-container op works on any FGameplayTagContainer property. append adds tags without disturbing existing ones. remove takes a single tag back out. clear empties the container entirely, and the default set op replaces the whole container: To add tags: properties: mGameplayTags: $op: append value: - MyOverhaul.Simple - KMods.WikiExclude To remove one tag: properties: mGameplayTags: $op: remove value: KMods.WikiExclude To empty or replace the container: properties: mGameplayTags: $op: clear properties: mGameplayTags: - MyOverhaul.Machines.Tier2 Choose one of these blocks for a given properties: mapping. To apply several operations to mGameplayTags in order, use the ordered list form instead.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - "Invalid tag" at load time: the error message includes the engine's own suggested fix, since this is usually a malformed dot-separated string with a stray space or an extra dot. Fix the string in your YAML, not the tag itself. There's nothing to "clean up" on the engine side. - A tag works this session but the pack is gone and it's still there: this is expected, since nothing is unregistered mid-session, and gameplay tags have no supported "remove" path. It will stop appearing on the _next_ full restart once the YAML is gone. - matchTag: finds nothing: double check that ofClass: is actually the class (or an ancestor of the class) the tag was applied to. Also check that the gametag document registering the tag is a .gametag.yml file, not accidentally named .cdo.yml, since KDataForge infers type: from the filename when type: itself is omitted.

sections.heading: Reference
sections.text: Registering your own tags, and using them the same pack over, is also part of the end-to-end walkthrough in End-to-End Pack. Bulk-editing content by tag is covered in Targeting → matchTag and Balancing.

pages.title: Type: item
pages.description: Generate item classes from YAML with the correct parent, class identity, and property defaults.

sections.heading: Type: item
sections.text: The item document type runs in the Items stage at priority 30, after class (50) and unlock (40), and before resource (25) and building (20). Documents load during GameInstance initialization. Restart the session after changing YAML. Entries live under the items key, and each one defaults to a parent of /Script/FactoryGame.FGItemDescriptor, which is also the required base class (or a subclass of it). Register-only mode (class:) is not supported here; items are always generated, so use id: instead. item creates a genuinely new UFGItemDescriptor-derived class at runtime. This is the same kind of class every base-game part or component is. It shares the entry grammar with resource, building, unlock, recipe, schematic, and research (see YAML Schema → Content Creation). However, item (along with resource, building, and unlock) can only _generate_ a class, never register an existing one. That register-only mode is reserved for recipe/schematic/research, see Recipes.

sections.heading: Minimal example
sections.text: A pack that wants a new tier-2 ingot needs exactly one items: entry. The id: field gives the class a stable identity, parent: seeds it from an existing item's mesh, icon, and form, and properties: overrides only what should actually differ: # file: super-ingot.item.yml type: item items: - id: MySuperIngot # required, stable id parent: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C # optional properties: # ordinary cdo-style ops mDisplayName: key: MySuperIngot_Name ns: MyPack source: Super Ingot mDescription: A far superior ingot. mStackSize: SS_HUGE # EStackSize enum see Balancing → Items for the full value list - id: is required and forms the save-persistence contract, see below. - parent: defaults to plain FGItemDescriptor if omitted. Giving an existing item's class (like Desc_IronIngot above) copies its mesh, icon, form, and category defaults, so properties: only needs to override what actually differs. - properties: uses the exact same op grammar as cdo patches. Every UFGItemDescriptor property is fair game. The common ones (mStackSize, mForm, mEnergyValue, mResourceSinkPoints, mCategory, mGameplayTags, …) are cataloged with more examples in Balancing → Items.

sections.heading: Generated class identity (the save-persistence contract)
sections.text: Every generated item lands in a deterministic package and class name, derived purely from the pack's ref and the entry's id:, never from file path or load order. That means the same YAML always regenerates the exact same class path on every load and across every machine: - The class lives in package /KDataForge/Gen/<PackRef> and is named Gen_<PackRef>_<Id>. This is deterministic and id-based, never derived from file path or load order. - Reference it from anywhere else (a recipe's mProduct, a schematic's mCost, a sinkpoints entry, another pack's YAML) as /KDataForge/Gen/<PackRef>.Gen_<PackRef>_<Id>. Or, from within the same pack (or if the id is unique across packs), just the bare id: itself, e.g. MySuperIngot. See Generated Content Short Ids. - Renaming the YAML file is always safe. Renaming the id: changes the generated class path, though, and that would orphan any save that already references it. Declare the rename as a redirects: entry in pack.yml instead (FCoreRedirects resolves the old path transparently). See End-to-End Pack → Renaming an id. - Classes are created at GameInstance INITIALIZATION, strictly before any save loads, so save data referencing them resolves correctly the moment the save starts loading. - Constraint: a generated class has exactly the parent's layout. There are no new reflected properties and no new components. All customisation lives in the CDO defaults properties: sets. If you need a building with a genuinely different mesh or a new component, reparent an existing buildable instead of trying to add one, see Buildings.

sections.heading: Why `Items` runs before `Recipes`/`Schematics`/`Research`
sections.text: class, unlock, item, resource, and building all generate in the same Items stage, priority-ordered as class → unlock → item → resource → building. This ordering exists specifically so that later stages can reference whatever they generated. For example, a recipe document can put a freshly generated item in its mProduct without any include:, because the Items stage has already finished by the time Recipes runs.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - "class: is only valid for recipe/schematic/research": you tried the register-only mode on an item entry. Items can only be generated (id:), never just registered from an existing class. If you already have a class you want KDataForge to leave alone, you don't need this document type for it at all. Just reference the class path directly wherever you'd otherwise reference the generated one. - Item generated fine, but a properties: entry silently didn't apply: this is the same as any cdo patch. Check /kdf report for a rejected op or a bad property key. Nothing about generation changes how property ops are validated. - Need this item in a recipe or schematic right away? No include: is needed, ever, see "Why Items runs before..." above. If a reference still fails to resolve, double-check the id spelling matches exactly (Gen_<PackRef>_<Id> is case-sensitive). - Made an item but don't see it anywhere in-game: this almost always means nothing unlocks it yet. An item and a recipe producing it are not enough on their own. Walk through Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock for the complete chain, including the schematic step that's usually missing.

pages.title: Localization and compiled translations
pages.description: Gather keyed YAML text into Unreal catalogs, compile mod translations, or inject translations for each runtime culture.

sections.heading: Localization and compiled translations
sections.text: KDataForge supports both the standard Unreal .po / .locres workflow for keyed YAML text and runtime translation documents (type: localization).

sections.heading: Compile YAML texts with Unreal localization
sections.text: Use this workflow when a mod already has a Localization Target and you want YAML-authored names, descriptions, or other keyed FText values included in its normal translation pipeline: type: cdo conditions: hasMod: - SatisfactoryPlus - KLib patches: - target: /KLib/Assets/Buildings/PressureRegulatorValve/Build_PressureRegulatorValve.Build_PressureRegulatorValve_C properties: mDisplayName: key: 895CFBF74588721183546EBD628AA06D ns: ST_Klib source: Pressure Trigger Valve The gather integration preserves ns, key, and the decoded source string, including line breaks, quotes, backslashes, Unicode, {VarName} placeholders, and literal percent characters. Keep these fields literal; the gather does not evaluate templates or execute runtime patches. A plain scalar value: Pressure Trigger Valve has no stable localization key and is not gathered by this integration. An omitted ns uses an empty namespace, matching the runtime text conversion. Pack display metadata supports the same text form. Keep stable keys when changing wording: ref: ExamplePack name: ns: ExamplePack key: Pack.Name source: Example Pack description: ns: ExamplePack key: Pack.Description source: Production adjustments for this mod. version: 1.0.0 Scalar names/descriptions remain compatible, but explicit keyed maps are required when those labels need compiled translations. The pack ref and dependency references are technical IDs.

sections.heading: Required target settings
sections.text: 1. Enable KDataForge and build its editor modules. Restart the editor after updating the plugin so KDataForgeLocalization is loaded. This editor module supports commandlets and is not needed in the packaged game. 2. Keep the mod's normal Localization Target, native language, translated languages, manifest and archive names. 3. Add CommandletClass=GatherKDataForgeText as a gather configuration step before GenerateGatherManifest. Keep existing source and asset steps for texts authored in C++ or Unreal assets. YAML gathering needs no h file filter, generated headers, or extra search path. 4. Run the target's checked-in gather configuration with UnrealEditor-Cmd -run=GatherText, then export PO files, translate/import them, and compile .locres. Existing Dashboard export/import/ compile actions and Tolgee workflows can use these same catalogs. Do not enable placeholder conversion. If Dashboard settings regenerate the gather configuration, retain or restore the dedicated KDF step before gathering again. 5. Package and load the mod's Localization Target as usual. The resulting .locres translates the keyed FText that KDataForge creates at runtime. The target name must match either the plugin name or a target declared in that plugin's .uplugin LocalizationTargets. Each matching target gathers the plugin's own pack texts. The YAML's namespace does not select its owning mod or target: in the example, a file shipped inside SatisfactoryPlus is gathered into the SatisfactoryPlus target even though its namespace is ST_Klib and its patch changes a KLib class. Use manifest dependencies if several targets share texts and you want Unreal to exclude already gathered entries. The integration discovers DataForge, legacy data-editor, and directories containing pack.yml under the owning plugin, and reads their .yml and .yaml files recursively, including nested packs, multi-document streams, and keyed text in pack.yml. Initial root discovery uses a recursion limit of six and skips engine/build directories such as Content, Source, Config, Intermediate, and Saved. Dot-prefixed directories, Docs, and Scripts are also excluded, both during root discovery and when collecting documents inside a root. Pack enabled flags, mod conditions, and runtime dependencies do not filter localization gathering: optional compatibility content needs translations even when its target mod is absent in the editor. YAML outside that plugin is not included. The KDF step adds each decoded native text directly to Unreal's gather manifest. Source references are stable, plugin-relative YAML locations such as DataForge/buildings/valve.cdo.yml:14, with the line pointing to the source value. No temporary headers or operating-system user paths enter manifest or PO references. Namespace, key, and decoded source text remain unchanged. Preview gathers include YAML when gathering Source or All, matching Unreal's source-text collector; Asset previews do not collect YAML.

sections.heading: Commandlet configuration
sections.text: Retain the normal manifest/archive/language settings. Add the dedicated KDF step before manifest creation; renumber any subsequent steps to keep a unique, increasing sequence: [GatherTextStep0] CommandletClass=GatherKDataForgeText [GatherTextStep1] CommandletClass=GenerateGatherManifest [GatherTextStep2] CommandletClass=GenerateGatherArchive This minimal example gathers only YAML. Keep existing GatherTextFromSource and GatherTextFromAssets steps when the target also owns C++ or asset texts. The SF+ configuration already includes all three collectors in the correct order. & 'C:/Program Files/Unreal Engine - CSS/Engine/Binaries/Win64/UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe' ` 'C:/Modding/FactoryGame.uproject' -run=GatherText ` '-config=C:/Modding/Mods/GameFeatures/SatisfactoryPlus/Config/Localization/SatisfactoryPlus_Gather.ini' ` -EnablePlugins=KDataForge -unattended ManifestName=SatisfactoryPlus.manifest identifies the SatisfactoryPlus target. The KDF plugin must be enabled in the commandlet process. Run normal export/import/compile steps afterward; adding .yml as a C++ source file filter is not a replacement for GatherKDataForgeText.

sections.heading: KMods CI/CD translation script
sections.text: The KMods workspace script includes YAML text gathering in its normal translation flow: # Same local stages as CI; pull translations without uploading or deleting Tolgee keys .\translation-scripts\sync_translation.ps1 -Plugins SatisfactoryPlus -SkipUpload # Local gather/export check without contacting Tolgee .\translation-scripts\sync_translation.ps1 -Plugins SatisfactoryPlus -LocalizationSteps "Gather,Export" -SkipTolgee Build FactoryEditor and the KDataForgeLocalization editor module before running the script. CI does this before translation sync. The gather command enables KDataForge explicitly and uses an effective config at exports/<Mod>/<Mod>_Gather.ini. Keep the dedicated GatherKDataForgeText step in each mod's checked-in gather configuration; the script preserves it. Its legacy source-gather and h-filter setup remains harmless for ordinary C++ texts but does not gather YAML by itself. Existing manifest identity, languages, dependencies, and asset gathering stay intact. The script does not rewrite saved gather settings. The script verifies the YAML bridge log and fails on missing bridge output, YAML errors, or failed gather/export/import/compile commands. CI stops before packaging when translation sync fails. Stage logs are under exports/, for example exports/SatisfactoryPlus_gather.log. -SkipUpload skips only the Tolgee upload and cleanup. It still gathers, exports, pulls, imports, and compiles by default. To reuse an existing manifest without gathering, request -LocalizationSteps "Import,Compile" explicitly. CI does not upload newly gathered source keys; run the normal sync without -SkipUpload separately to make those keys available in Tolgee. After gathering/exporting, the current native English PO is retained when copying pulled translations, so a Tolgee download cannot replace freshly gathered YAML source keys. With -SkipUpload, only cloud translations matching the current exported source are imported. Retired cloud keys are excluded; new or untranslated entries keep the native-language fallback. Normal upload sync retains strict source-parity checks.

sections.heading: Gather diagnostics
sections.text: The log category LogKDFLocalization reports how many YAML files supplied text for each target. An entry such as Target 'SatisfactoryPlus': injected localization sources from 1 YAML file(s) confirms that the native YAML gather step ran. A second log entry reports the keyed text count. Check the exported PO for your namespace/key and the actual relative YAML location before uploading it for translation. There is no generated .h file to ship or edit. Malformed/unreadable YAML and conflicting source strings for the same namespace/key produce errors. Resolve these before importing or compiling translations. Conflicts with gathered asset or C++ texts also use Unreal's normal conflict reporting. Empty source strings are not gathered. If no gather log appears, check that the plugin/editor module is loaded, the configuration includes GatherKDataForgeText before manifest generation, and the target name belongs to the mod. A source gather step alone no longer creates temporary YAML headers. Targets without KDF pack roots retain a zero-file receipt for compatibility with existing workspace pipeline checks. Changing a source string can invalidate an older translation because Unreal checks the source hash. Re-gather and translate the changed source. Avoid reusing another mod's namespace/key for different text unless you deliberately intend to override that shared identity.

sections.heading: Runtime translation documents
sections.text: type: localization injects translations directly into the running localization manager without compiling .locres. These translation documents are not gathered as native texts by the native gather integration; use keyed FText maps in your content documents for the compiled workflow above. The Localization stage runs after GameTags/Assets and before CDOChanges. Its entries key is entries, a map from key to either a scalar or a block map with source and text fields.

sections.heading: Simple key entries: new text
sections.text: The scalar form registers a brand new localized text under namespace: and key. This works for your own content's FText keys, or anyone else's, as long as the namespace and key match: # file: de.localization.yml type: localization namespace: MyPack culture: de # prefix-matched: also applies for de-DE, de-AT, … entries: MySuperIngot_Name: 'Superbarren' MySuperIngot_Desc: 'Ein weit überlegener Barren.'

sections.heading: `source` + `text` map: overriding an EXISTING text
sections.text: The map form overrides a text that already exists (vanilla or modded) by its original source string: type: localization namespace: MyPack culture: de entries: IronIngot_Renamed: source: 'Iron Ingot' text: 'Eisenbarren (überarbeitet)' SchematicOverride: source: 'Super Ingot Smelting' text: 'Superbarren-Verhüttung' > ⚠️ Source-hash matching. UE identifies a localized text by its namespace/key plus a hash of > the original source string. The source: you give must be byte-identical to the current > original text: spacing, punctuation, and capitalisation all matter. If a game update changes > the source string, the override silently stops matching. Copy the exact string from the game, > don't retype it. Omitting source: uses text: as the source too, which only works for > new keys. The scalar form above is the same thing written shorter.

sections.heading: How it's applied
sections.text: Localization entries are applied through the same mechanism the engine's own localization system uses to load .locres files, so there is nothing KDataForge-specific for the game to special-case.

sections.heading: Bidirectional prefix matching for `culture:`
sections.text: culture: de # matches current language de, de-DE, de-AT, … For a regional variant: culture: pt-BR # matches only pt-BR (a more specific prefix than pt) Omit culture: to apply entries for every language. The match is bidirectional prefix matching: either the current language starts with culture:, or culture: starts with the current language. culture: de applies when the running game is set to de-DE, and culture: de-DE would also apply if the game were set to plain de. Whichever side is the shorter prefix wins the comparison. In practice, prefer the shortest culture code that covers your translation, de rather than de-DE, unless you specifically need a regional variant. Documents whose culture: doesn't match the current language are skipped with an Info diagnostic. This is not a warning: it's expected, not an error.

sections.heading: Loading changes
sections.text: Localization changes are loaded on the next session start. A complete worked translation (item + schematic + German locale file, applied together) is part of the end-to-end pack in End-to-End Pack.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - My override isn't taking effect. This is almost always the source-hash mismatch described above. Copy the original string straight out of the game, or the base-game source if you have it, rather than retyping it from memory. A single missing period or extra space is enough to break the match silently. - Translation shows in one culture but not another. Check for a stray culture: on the file. Omitting it entirely is usually what you want, unless you're intentionally splitting translations per locale across files. - New key works, but overriding an existing key doesn't. New keys, using the scalar form, don't need source: to match anything since there's nothing to match yet. Overrides, using the map form, do need it. If you're not sure which one you need, ask yourself: does this text already exist in the game?

pages.title: Operations
pages.description: Choose among 25 property operations, check supported property kinds, and follow a working example for each operation.

sections.heading: Operations
sections.text: Write properties: as a mapping from property paths to values. A plain value performs set, replacing the current value. Add $op inside a property's value to choose another operation and pass its arguments: properties: mDisplayNameOverride: true mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.5 mIngredients: $op: append value: ItemClass: /Game/Example/Desc_Item.Desc_Item_C Amount: 4 The mapping form also works in generated content and instanced-object properties: blocks. A nested struct mapping is a plain set value unless it contains $op directly. Use the ordered path/value list when one property needs several operations, because YAML mapping keys cannot repeat. Both forms use the same operations and argument names; see YAML Schema. For a condition on one operation, use a conditional patch entry or the legacy list form; conditions: is not a field inside a mapped $op value. The 25 operations are grouped by the kind of property they act on: numeric math and clamping, container mutation for arrays, sets, maps, and tag containers, string concatenation, array reordering and deduplication, and cross-property copy or move. See Patching (type: cdo) for the full patch structure these entries live inside. See Property Types for what each underlying property looks like in YAML.

sections.heading: Select every gameplay tag container
sections.text: Use the quoted operation path '@tagContainers' to apply the same operation to every top-level FGameplayTagContainer on each target. Inherited fields are included. With applyToSubclasses: true, KDF selects fields again for each subclass, including additional fields on classes loaded later. An object without matching fields is a no-op. type: cdo patches: - target: /Script/FactoryGame.FGResourceDescriptor applyToSubclasses: true properties: '@tagContainers': $op: append value: - KMods.PlannerResource Register tags before using them, for example through a type: gametag document. Supported operations are set (also the default), append, prepend, remove and clear. Tag containers are sets: adding an existing tag does not create duplicates. Each selected field gets its own normal snapshot and patch record for rollback. Use consecutive remove and append entries in the ordered list form to replace one set of tags with another. The selector does not recurse into nested structs, objects or arrays and cannot be combined with a suffix such as .Child or [0]. It is only an operation destination, not a concrete property path for where, from, templates or single-property read/edit APIs. Use an actual field name in those contexts. Keep quotes: YAML does not allow an unquoted scalar starting with @.

sections.heading: append_unique: array
sections.text: Appends each incoming value only if no equal element is already present. Existing duplicates and their order stay unchanged; repeated incoming values are added at most once. This matches a MergeUnique-style update without deduplicating the destination array: mAllowedResourceForms: $op: append_unique value: - RF_GAS For example, an array with two RF_LIQUID entries gains one RF_GAS entry. Applying the same operation again leaves it unchanged. value accepts one element or a sequence; an empty sequence is a successful no-op. Equality uses the reflected element type, including enum, struct and object identity. Arrays only: use ordinary append for sets/maps. Subobject definitions with class and properties creation is rejected; reference an existing object or use append to create a new instance. Malformed operands fail without leaving a partial array edit.

sections.heading: update_where: array of structs
sections.text: update_where checks every struct element in an array and partially updates every match. The where path is relative to one element, not the patched object. value must be a struct mapping; members omitted from that mapping keep their current values: mProduct: $op: update_where where: path: ItemClass equals: /OldMod/Items/Desc_Old.Desc_Old_C value: ItemClass: /NewMod/Items/Desc_New.Desc_New_C Use a sequence under where for several clauses. They use AND by default. Set sibling whereMode: OR to update an element when any clause matches: mProduct: $op: update_where whereMode: OR where: - path: ItemClass equals: Desc_OldA_C - path: ItemClass equals: Desc_OldB_C value: ItemClass: Desc_New_C whereMode accepts AND or OR case-insensitively and requires where. Clauses accept the same operators as target filters: equals, notEquals, numeric comparisons, contains, notContains, in, notIn, matches, and isEmpty. Nested paths and [*] reads are supported inside the element. Every matching element is updated. No match is an error, protecting patches against upstream array changes. Invalid predicates or values roll back the whole array operation; partial writes are not kept. Only arrays whose elements are reflected structs are supported. This operation is useful for recipe mIngredients and mProduct arrays because it does not depend on element order.

sections.heading: replace_refs: reflected reference trees
sections.text: replace_refs searches below one property and replaces every exact matching object or class reference. It follows reflected structs, arrays, sets, maps, and instanced objects. This makes the same operation usable for recipe inputs/outputs and for nested schematic unlock or dependency objects without knowing array indexes or concrete unlock subclasses: mUnlocks: $op: replace_refs from: /OldMod/Recipes/Recipe_Old.Recipe_Old_C value: /NewMod/Recipes/Recipe_New.Recipe_New_C Use mIngredients: or mProduct: as the mapping key for recipes, mUnlocks: for unlock payloads, mSchematicDependencies: for schematic dependencies, or mTaskDependencies: for KAPI delivery-task dependencies. The selected property is also the traversal boundary: unrelated properties on the target are never searched. Both hard and soft object/class references are supported. Instanced objects are traversed, but KDF does not follow ordinary external object references into unrelated assets. from and value must be scalar references. The replacement must satisfy every matched property's reflected class type. Zero matches, incompatible targets, or excessive nesting fail the operation. All matched references are validated before writing; a failure keeps original values.

sections.heading: set (default): everything
sections.text: set overwrites the property outright. It works on any property type, which is why it can be left implicit. On mDisplayName (an FString), setting a value replaces the string: mDisplayName: 'Reinforced Iron Ingot' # set is implied

sections.heading: Bitmask operations
sections.text: set accepts one flag name or a sequence of flag names. KDataForge resolves and ORs names from the property's BitmaskEnum. Raw numeric masks are accepted by set only. Plain integer bitmask handling requires WITH_METADATA, retained property metadata, and an already-loaded enum; missing metadata or an unresolved enum leaves ordinary integer conversion. See Property Types for named mask/index forms, width limits, and Shipping-build limitations. For one flag: mParentTask: Above For several flags: mParentTask: - Above - Left

sections.heading: add / subtract: numeric
sections.text: add and subtract do in-place arithmetic on a plain numeric property. They add or subtract value from whatever is currently stored. Both reject enum-backed integers (see the callout below), since there is no meaningful "current + 1" for an enum ordinal: mTechTier: $op: add value: 1 mTimeToComplete: $op: subtract value: 30

sections.heading: multiply / divide: numeric
sections.text: multiply and divide scale a numeric property by value. Setting mManufactoringDuration to a fraction of itself halves the crafting time, while dividing mEnergyValue doubles the effective fuel efficiency. Dividing by 0 is rejected outright, rather than producing infinity or NaN: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.5 mEnergyValue: $op: divide value: 2

sections.heading: min / max: numeric (result = min/max of current and value)
sections.text: min enforces a ceiling: the property is replaced with whichever is smaller, the current value or value. max enforces a floor, replacing the property with whichever is larger. Neither can push the property past value in the opposite direction, which makes them useful for "never exceed" or "never fall below" balancing passes across many objects at once: To cap sink points at 100: mResourceSinkPoints: $op: min value: 100 To raise them to at least 50: mResourceSinkPoints: $op: max value: 50 To enforce both bounds in one mapping entry, use clamp with min: 50 and max: 100. :::caution Enum-backed properties don't count as numeric. mStackSize on FGItemDescriptor is an EStackSize enum (SS_ONE…SS_HUGE/SS_FLUID), not a plain int min/max/clamp/ add/subtract/multiply/divide are all rejected on it (op not supported); only set with an enum value name works. See Property Types → Enums. :::

sections.heading: clamp: numeric
sections.text: clamp is the two-sided version of min/max: instead of a single value, it takes min and max keys and pins the current value inside that range in one step: mMenuPriority: $op: clamp min: 0 max: 999

sections.heading: append: array / set / map / string / tag container / bitmask
sections.text: append adds to the end of a container, or concatenates onto a string. It behaves differently depending on the target property's kind. For arrays and sets, value can be a single item or a sequence to add several items at once. For strings, it concatenates text. For tag containers, it adds tags. For maps, value must be a map, and KDataForge merges those key/value pairs into the existing map: # array: adds element(s) at the end mIngredients: $op: append value: ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/Coal/Desc_Coal.Desc_Coal_C Amount: 1 # string: concatenates mDisplayName: $op: append value: ' (rebalanced)' # tag container: adds tags mGameplayTags: $op: append value: - MyPack.Rebalanced # map: merges entries mSomeMap: $op: append value: Iron: 10 # bitmask: OR-adds flags mParentTask: $op: append value: - Above - Left For bitmasks, append ORs named flags into current mask. It does not accept raw integer masks. For instanced UObject arrays, an appended value can be a map with class and nested properties; KDataForge constructs the new subobject before inserting it into the array: mUnlocks: $op: append value: class: /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties: mRecipes: - Recipe_MyGeneratedRecipe :::note String operations on FText properties (like mDisplayName when it is a localized text field) produce plain culture-invariant text the original localization key/namespace is dropped, so an append/prepend/clear on a translated string stops it from tracking further translation updates. See Localization if you need the result to stay localizable instead. :::

sections.heading: prepend: array / set / string (tag containers and bitmasks: same as append)
sections.text: prepend mirrors append, but it adds at the front instead of the end for arrays, and inserts before the existing text for strings. Tag containers treat it identically to append, since a tag container has no ordering. Sets also treat it like append, because sets have no ordering. Bitmasks also treat it like append and OR-add named flags. Maps do not support prepend at all: only append merges into a map. mDisplayName: $op: prepend value: '[MP] '

sections.heading: insert: array
sections.text: insert places one or more elements at a specific index inside an array, rather than always at the end, and shifts later elements back. An out-of-range index fails with an error, instead of clamping to the array's bounds. Instanced UObject array entries may use the same `{ class, properties } map accepted by set, append, and prepend`: mIngredients: $op: insert index: 1 value: ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/OreCopper/Desc_OreCopper.Desc_OreCopper_C Amount: 1

sections.heading: remove: array (by value) / set (by value) / map (by key) / tag container / bitmask
sections.text: remove deletes by content rather than by position. On arrays and sets, it deletes every element that matches value exactly. An array remove that matches nothing fails, rather than silently doing nothing. On maps, value is the _key_ to delete, and on tag containers, value is the tag (or list of tags) to remove. On bitmasks, it clears every named bit with AND-NOT: # removes every element equal to the value mIngredients: $op: remove value: ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/OreIron/Desc_OreIron.Desc_OreIron_C Amount: 1 # map: value is the key mSomeMap: $op: remove value: Iron mGameplayTags: $op: remove value: KMods.WikiExclude # bitmask: clears named bits mParentTask: $op: remove value: Left

sections.heading: remove_at: array
sections.text: remove_at deletes the element at a specific position instead of matching by value. It is the right tool when you know the slot but not, or don't want to spell out, the exact contents: mProduct: $op: remove_at index: 1

sections.heading: clear: array / set / map / string / tag container / bitmask
sections.text: clear empties a container-shaped property entirely: arrays, sets, maps, and tag containers all lose every element. Strings are reset to empty, rather than to their class-default text. On a metadata-recognized bitmask, clear writes 0: mSubCategories: $op: clear # bitmask: sets mask to 0 mParentTask: $op: clear

sections.heading: swap: array
sections.text: swap exchanges the elements at two positions, index and with, in an array without touching anything else in the list. It is useful for reordering a couple of entries without rewriting the whole array: mIngredients: $op: swap index: 0 with: 1

sections.heading: replace: array
sections.text: replace overwrites the element at index with a new value, keeping every other element and the array's length unchanged: mProduct: $op: replace index: 0 value: ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/SteelIngot/Desc_SteelIngot.Desc_SteelIngot_C Amount: 2

sections.heading: duplicate: array (copies element to the end)
sections.text: duplicate copies the element at index and appends the copy to the end of the same array. It is handy for cloning an existing ingredient or product entry as a starting point, before tweaking it with a follow-up replace: mProduct: $op: duplicate index: 0

sections.heading: sort / reverse: array
sections.text: sort reorders an array in ascending order. Numeric and string inner types sort by their actual value. Anything else, such as structs or object references, sorts by its exported text form. reverse flips the current order of every element: # numeric/string inner types sort by value; others by text form mRelevantEvents: $op: sort mSubCategories: $op: reverse

sections.heading: unique: array (removes later duplicates; sets: no-op)
sections.text: unique walks an array and removes any element that is byte-identical to an earlier one, keeping the first occurrence of each value. Running it on a set is always a no-op, since a set is already guaranteed to contain no duplicates: mSubCategories: $op: unique

sections.heading: copy: any property (from another path on the same object)
sections.text: copy reads the value at another property path (from) on the same object and writes it into the target property. When source and destination are exactly the same property type, it copies the raw value directly. Otherwise, it round-trips through each property's text representation. This means copying between compatible but different types, for example a plain string into a name, can still work, as long as the text parses back cleanly for the destination type: mAbbreviatedDisplayName: $op: copy from: mDisplayName

sections.heading: move: copy, then reset the source to its default
sections.text: move performs the exact same copy as copy, then clears the source property back to its default value. This makes it the right choice when a value should live at the new path _instead of_ the old one, rather than in both places: mDescription: $op: move from: mScannerDisplayText

pages.title: Pack configuration
pages.description: Define typed pack settings, read player values, and control when a changed setting takes effect.

sections.heading: Pack configuration
sections.text: A *.config.yml or *.config.yaml file defines settings offered by a pack. Use type: config and a non-empty fields list. Definitions load separately from the player's values, stored under FactoryGame/Configs/Packs/<PackRef>.config.yml. Keep the pack's ref stable; packs defining configuration need a ref of at most 50 characters.

sections.heading: Removing obsolete configuration
sections.text: After a successful definition load, KDataForge rewrites the pack's values file using its current fields. Values of remaining fields are retained; removed fields and their empty groups disappear, including legacy __sounds entries. Renaming a field creates a new key and removes the old key; migrate any values you need before renaming it. Generated FactoryGame/Configs/Packs/<PackRef>.config.yml files are removed when their pack is no longer installed or no longer defines configuration. This happens after pack discovery and definition processing, including on reload. Installed packs that are disabled or skipped because of dependencies remain known and keep their files. Configuration documents skipped by conditions retain their stored keys rather than being mistaken for removed fields. Deletion only targets direct *.config.yml files carrying the generated # KDataForge pack configuration header and containing valid YAML mappings. Unmarked or unreadable files are left untouched. Discovery warnings or errors prevent file deletion for that load. Invalid or partially skipped definitions prevent obsolete-field pruning for their pack. Read-only editor registries never write or delete values files. Host-replicated values do not trigger local cleanup. # file: balance.config.yml type: config category: /Script/FactoryGame.FGCategory fields: - id: balance.duration type: number valueType: float name: Production duration description: Recipe duration in seconds used by this pack's patches. default: 1 min: 0.25 max: 4 step: 0.25 display: slider apply: hot The category above uses the base category. For a named settings section, use a category subclass as described below. A field with an error is skipped while other valid fields can still load. Static document conditions are supported; configuration definitions cannot depend on config: conditions themselves.

sections.heading: Blueprint pack lists
sections.text: For settings widgets, Get All Pack Infos returns only packs with at least one authored configuration field. Sound-volume controls belong only to the local Audio settings and do not make a pack appear in this list. Packs with no valid fields are omitted. Active packs appear in load order, with the first loaded pack first. Dependencies load before their dependents; among packs ready to load, higher priority comes first, then ref alphabetically. Inactive packs follow the active entries, sorted by ref. Filter on mState when the widget should display only active packs, and keep the returned array order rather than sorting it again. Get Pack Info(PackRef) can still look up a specific pack without configuration fields.

sections.heading: Ready-made Blueprint settings widgets
sections.text: KDataForge's runtime UI module provides native C++ widgets using FactoryGame's options-row, checkbox, slider, dropdown, font and status-icon assets. Rows keep the original 300-pixel control column. Checkbox and slider rows use the 33-pixel baseline; text and number inputs use 40 pixels. Text inputs use FactoryGame's dark input background, left-aligned font and orange hover/focus border. Apply, Discard, Add and Remove use FactoryGame's standard buttons, including their native interaction states. Reset retains the compact options icon. Multiline text, tags and collections expand vertically. Use an automatically sized panel slot; a fixed 33-pixel slot would clip these controls. The released 2026.4.582 settings page requires KUI. The upcoming development release moves the category, empty-state, and styled tooltip visuals into KDataForge itself and removes that runtime KUI requirement. In a Widget Blueprint: Get Config Descriptions Flat (PackRef) → For Each → Create Config Widget (Description = Array Element) → Add Child to your panel Create Config Widget automatically chooses the matching class. You can also use Create Widget with a specific class and connect its exposed Description pin: | Description kind | Widget class | | Text, including multiline text | KDFConfigTextWidget | | Gameplay tag | KDFConfigTagWidget | | Number input | KDFConfigNumberWidget | | Slider | KDFConfigSliderWidget | | Boolean | KDFConfigBooleanWidget | | Select | KDFConfigSelectWidget | | Multi-select | KDFConfigMultiSelectWidget | | Text, number or tag list | KDFConfigListWidget | The row manages its label, tooltip, current value, validation errors, default reset, pending-change indicator and restart notices. Multiplayer clients without edit permission see disabled controls. Tags offer registered-tag suggestions and an editable path; lists support adding, removing and editing entries within their configured limits. Edits remain pending. Reset to default also creates a pending change. Apply pack changes saves all pending edits of the description's pack; Discard pack changes discards that pack's pending edits. These actions include edits in sibling rows. Hot settings follow the normal KDataForge reload rules; cold settings show the restart requirement. Dedicated-server admin requests keep the pack's controls disabled until all request chunks finish, including errors and timeouts. For a menu with one shared footer, pass Show Apply Discard = false, or call Set Show Actions(false) on its rows. Connect the menu's buttons to Apply Changes and Discard Changes on any row belonging to that pack. The widget checks validation errors in the pack's other visible rows before applying. Calling the lower-level Apply Config Changes(PackRef) directly does not inspect unfinished widget input. For a shared Reset All button, call Reset Pack Config To Default(PackRef). It stages each editable field's default without saving or reloading. Pass an empty PackRef to reset all packs. Read-only fields remain unchanged; an unknown pack or unavailable subsystem does nothing. Apply or discard the staged reset through the same menu actions as other pending edits. Use the pure Blueprint node Is Pack Config Dirty(PackRef) to enable a shared Apply button. It returns whether that pack has unsaved pending values; an empty PackRef checks all packs. An unknown pack or unavailable subsystem returns false. Has Pending Config Changes remains available with the same behavior. For updates without polling, call Get KDataForge Subsystem and bind to On Pack Config Changed. The event supplies Pack Ref and Is Dirty; filter the reference for the pack displayed by your menu. It fires on configuration value or state changes, including edits, reset, apply, discard and reload, even when the dirty flag stays unchanged. Deferred load events are grouped per pack. After binding, read Is Pack Config Dirty once to initialize the button. Unbind your listener when the menu closes. For a menu spanning all packs, query Is Pack Config Dirty with an empty reference after each event. The row also exposes Apply Changes, Discard Changes, Reset to Default, Get Validation Error and On Applied. On Applied reports the initial pending result for an admin request, then the combined result after every chunk completes. Keep the row's Description reference instead of copying configuration values into unrelated widget variables. Reloads refresh labels, constraints and values. Removed fields disable their rows. If an author changes a field's kind during development, rebuild the menu with Create Config Widget to obtain the new matching widget class.

sections.heading: Preview in the Unreal Editor
sections.text: With the KDataForge UI module loaded, use the editor console to preview config definitions from a pack directory without starting PIE or writing saved values: KDF.Config.PreviewWidgets "C:/MyMod/DataForge" The preview allows pending-value edits and resets, but omits Apply/Discard because it does not represent a running pack. Actual saving, hot reload and multiplayer permissions must be checked in a game session.

sections.heading: Field types at a glance
sections.text: | type | valueType choices | Default valueType | Shape | | text | string, text, name, tag | string | String, or string list with multiple: true | | number | int8, int16, int32, int64, uint8, float, double | int32 | Number, or number list with multiple: true | | boolean | bool, uint8 | bool | Boolean; multiple is not supported | | select | All text and number types above, plus bool | string | One option value, or list with multiple: true |

sections.heading: Common field keys
sections.text: Every field requires id, type, name, description and default. | Key | Meaning | | id | Stable dotted identifier, such as balance.duration; used to read the value. | | type | Control family from the table above. | | valueType | Stored element type; defaults depend on type. | | name, description | Non-empty display text, either a string or keyed localized text. | | default | Initial value satisfying the field's type and constraints; a list when multiple: true. | | tooltip | Optional map containing title, text, or both; each accepts localized text. | | category | Category class for this field; overrides the document category. Required at one of these levels. | | apply | cold by default, or hot; see application rules below. | | order | Integer sort position within its category; otherwise declaration order across config files sorted by path. | | multiple | Enables lists for text and number, or multi-selection for select; defaults to false. | Identifiers use ASCII segments matching [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*, separated by dots, and may contain at most 200 characters. They must be unique across the pack's config files, ignoring case. An id cannot also be the dotted prefix of another id: do not define both balance and balance.duration. The identifiers true, false, in and contains are reserved; the __sounds namespace is reserved for compatibility with older sound controls. Dotted ids become nested maps in the saved values file. descriptionClass and field-level properties are reserved. The schema accepts them, but the runtime ignores them and reports a warning. They do not create custom controls or patch game properties.

sections.heading: Categories
sections.text: Set category on the document as the default, or on individual fields. It must resolve to a UFGCategory subclass. Accepted forms include a class path, a bare id of a class generated in the same pack, or its full generated path: /KDataForge/Gen/<PackRef>.Gen_<PackRef>_<Id>. Settings sections sort by the category's mMenuPriority. An unresolved or incorrect class produces an error and falls back to the base UFGCategory bucket. Create category subclasses with Type: class.

sections.heading: Numbers
sections.text: | Key | Constraint or behavior | | min, max | Optional inclusive bounds; min cannot exceed max. Values outside these bounds are clamped. | | step | Positive control increment; a whole number for integer types. | | decimals | Fractional digits shown and stored, from 0 to 9. Otherwise inferred from step, or defaults to 4 for float and 6 for double. | | display | slider or input. An explicit slider requires min < max and cannot use multiple: true. | Without display, a scalar field with both bounds and min < max becomes a slider; other number fields use an input. Integer types require integer defaults, bounds and steps. For lists, numeric constraints apply to each element.

sections.heading: Text, tags and selections
sections.text: Text fields accept maxLength from 1 to 1024, defaulting to 1024. Use multiline: true only with type: text and valueType: text. With valueType: tag, tagRoot restricts values to that gameplay-tag root; tags need not already be registered when configuration is read. Text and number lists use minCount and maxCount; lists hold at most 64 elements, with maxCount defaulting to 64. These count keys require multiple: true. Select fields require a non-empty options list. Each option has a unique value matching the field's valueType and a display label. The default must be one of those values, or a list of option values for a multi-select. Text option values are case-sensitive. type: config category: /Script/FactoryGame.FGCategory fields: - id: features.mode type: select name: Feature mode description: Choose which variant the pack uses. default: standard options: - value: standard label: Standard - value: extended label: Extended Multi-selects use minSelected and maxSelected instead of the list count keys. The minimum cannot exceed the number of options, and the maximum cannot be below the minimum or exceed 64.

sections.heading: Reading values
sections.text: Other documents can read a typed value with cfg:<id>, or cfg:<PackRef>:<id> to name another pack explicitly. String templates support {cfg:<id>} substitutions, and config: conditions can use configuration expressions. Configuration definitions themselves cannot use those conditions. For example, a property operation can consume the slider above directly: # Inside a patch's properties mapping: mManufactoringDuration: cfg:balance.duration This assigns the configured number to the recipe's duration property.

sections.heading: Hot and cold values
sections.text: apply: cold is the default. Applying a changed value saves it, but running content keeps the value used during its initial load. The runtime reports that a restart is required. apply: hot saves changes and triggers a KDataForge content reload when hot values change. The reload can update consumers during the current session. Whether the game actually uses a changed property immediately depends on that property and its consuming system. A hot field used in a cold context or cold property is flagged with a restart recommendation.

sections.heading: Cold properties
sections.text: Configuration application mode and property reload classification are separate. Reflection exports classify class properties as hot, cold or newActors: - hot: explicitly classified as applying live. - cold: read once or during object creation; changing it does not refresh existing state. - newActors: class-default changes affect newly spawned actors or components; a patch can use applyToSpawnedActors: true to include existing actors. The editor reports cold and newActors operations as property.cold. Catalog entries marked verified: false remain assumptions awaiting game verification. See Reflection Export for the kdf.reload, kdf.reloadReason and cold-property catalog fields.

sections.heading: Localized names
sections.text: Field names, descriptions, tooltip titles and texts, and select labels accept the keyed text form: name: key: Config_Speed_Name ns: MyPack source: Production duration Provide translations through Type: localization using the same namespace and key. When overriding existing source text, preserve the exact source string required by Unreal's source-hash matching. These display texts do not change field ids or stored option values.

sections.heading: Pack name, description and icon
sections.text: pack.yml supplies the pack's display name, description and optional icon. The runtime falls back to the pack ref when the name is absent; the editor schema requires a name. The description accepts either a string or keyed localized text. An icon can be a UTexture2D object path beginning with /, or a pack-relative png, jpg, jpeg, tga or bmp file. Relative files must remain inside the pack folder. Image-file limits are 16 MB and 4096 × 4096 pixels. Dedicated servers skip icon loading.

pages.title: Patching (type: cdo)
pages.description: Patch reflected properties with `type: cdo`, target selectors, and modifiers.

sections.heading: Patching (type: cdo)
sections.text: This document type runs at the CDOChanges stage, after GameTags, Assets, and Localization, and before any content-generation stage. Its entries live under the patches key as a sequence. After saving YAML changes, run /kdf reload on the host or KDF.Reload in the host/server console, then /kdf report to inspect the new load. Use this document type to edit any reflected property on any class default object or object instance in the game: items, recipes, buildings, schematics, research trees, KAPI/RRDA data assets, your own generated content, anything. Everything else this framework does (content creation, data assets, sink points) either patches through this same mechanism internally or exists alongside it.

sections.heading: Shape of a patch entry
sections.text: A type: cdo document is just a patches: list. Each entry needs at least one target selector (target:, allAssetsOfClass:, or an ofClass: scope with filters such as matchTag:, matchName:, producedIn:, where:), optional modifiers, and a properties: mapping describing the actual edits. The example below halves mManufactoringDuration on the iron ingot recipe: type: cdo patches: - # ---- one or more selectors are accepted; prefer one clear selector ---- target: /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C # target: also accepts a sequence of paths, patching every entry with the same properties: # OR: allAssetsOfClass: ... # OR: ofClass: ... + filters (matchTag / matchName / producedIn / ingredient / product / where) # ---- modifiers (all optional) ---- applyToSubclasses: false applyToSpawnedActors: false # ---- the ops ---- properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.5 Each entry needs at least one selector and a non-empty properties: block. The current implementation accumulates matches when selectors are combined, but one selector per entry is easier to audit. One document can hold any number of patch entries.

sections.heading: Hard asset references in native defaults
sections.text: Use full asset object paths for hard-reference properties such as TArray<TObjectPtr<UStaticMesh>>. A YAML sequence replaces the array; string allowlists remain ordinary strings. For example, with Periodic Madness installed: type: cdo patches: - target: /Script/PeriodicMadness.PMCleanerSettings properties: mStaticMeshesCleanlist: - /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/RawResources/Nodes/ResourceNode_OreIron_01.ResourceNode_OreIron_01 KDataForge keeps hard references added to permanent native defaults alive across garbage collection and session changes. These assets remain resident until the game exits, even if a later edit removes them from the array. No YAML opt-in or class declaration change is needed. After upgrading from a build where inspecting these arrays crashed, fully restart the game before loading the pack again.

sections.heading: Inline instances in property arrays
sections.text: An ordinary properties: entry can replace an array of instanced UObject references. Write each array entry as a map with class: and optional nested properties:. KDataForge creates the instance as a subobject of the patched target, then applies the nested property operations. This works for any compatible instanced object array, including schematic dependencies and unlocks. Because set is the default operation, the following patch replaces the complete mSchematicDependencies array on every target.
