pages.description: An ordered, top-to-bottom checklist for "my YAML file doesn't seem to be doing anything." Six checkpoints, from file discovery to reload verification.

sections.heading: Debug a pack that won't apply
sections.text: Use this checklist top to bottom when a pack does not apply and you do not yet know why. Each step rules out one pipeline stage before you move to the next. Document-specific symptoms remain in the Troubleshooting sections under Features. The first five steps follow the pipeline (Source/KDataForge/Private/Subsystems/KDFSubsystem.cpp): scan → parse/type-detect → conditions → validate → apply. Step 6 checks reload scope when testing YAML changes. After each saved edit, run /kdf reload on the host or KDF.Reload in the host/server console, then /kdf report before comparing diagnostics or counts.

sections.heading: Step 1: is the file even being scanned?
sections.text: KDataForge starts at the Unreal project root, which is FactoryGame/ in a packaged game, and walks up to 6 levels deep. A directory becomes a pack root when it is named DataForge, uses the legacy name data-editor, or directly contains pack.yml. Names are case-insensitive. While walking, the scanner prunes Content, Saved, Intermediate, Binaries, DerivedDataCache, Plugins, Source, and Config, so a root nested inside one of those directories is never found. It also ignores directories named Docs or Scripts and all directories whose names start with ., both during root discovery and inside detected packs. Keep authored YAML outside these directories. Outside those ignored development directories, files below a detected root are scanned for *.yml and *.yaml. pack.yml is read separately as the manifest. Roots may nest; each file belongs to its deepest enclosing root, never both the child and parent pack. Run /kdf report. The first line is always: KDataForge: N pack(s), N document(s) applied, N op(s), N actor patch(es), N error(s), N warning(s) - If the pack count didn't change after adding your folder, it wasn't found. Check the exact root marker (DataForge, data-editor, or a direct pack.yml), its depth from the project root, and that no parent directory in the path matches the pruned list above. - A pack directory that resolves but has enabled: false in pack.yml is excluded from the pack count entirely. It's never added to the pack list, and it produces only an Info-level "Pack '...' is disabled, skipped" diagnostic. See Step 3 for why that won't show up in the report text either. A disabled pack therefore looks identical, from the report's perspective, to a pack that was never found at all. - Two packs resolving to the same ref: the second directory is skipped entirely with a Warning, "Duplicate pack ref '...', directory skipped." This _is_ visible in /kdf report. If your pack doesn't even move the pack/document counts, nothing past this point matters yet. Fix the location first.

sections.heading: Step 2: did the root type resolve?
sections.text: First confirm the file parsed. Malformed YAML is an Error; that file is skipped, while every other file continues through the load. Fix the YAML parse failed diagnostic before checking its root type. A document's type comes from either an explicit type: key or the <name>.<type>.yml filename convention (e.g. super-ingot.item.yml implies type: item). There are two distinct ways this can go wrong, and they look different in the report. No type could be determined at all happens when there's no type: key and the filename doesn't match the convention either. This produces one Warning per offending file, from ScanAndParse: [Warning] my-pack/mystery-item.yml: No 'type:' key and no '<name>.<type>.yml' filename convention document skipped A type was determined, but no handler owns it happens with a typo like type: reciept, a <name>.reciept.yml filename, or a type that belongs to a mod you don't have loaded. This warns only once per distinct type string across the entire load, not once per file: [Warning] my-pack/typo.reciept.yml: No handler registered for document type 'reciept' (planned for a later phase?) That dedup matters. If you copy-pasted the same typo into five files, you'll only see one warning line, not five, so don't assume only the reported file is affected. Both lines follow FKDFDiagnostic::ToString()'s exact contract: [Severity] file: message, or [Severity] file:line: message when a line number is known. Most scan/type diagnostics don't carry one, since they're about the file as a whole, not one YAML node.

sections.heading: Step 3: did conditions pass?
sections.text: A conditions: object or array (gameVersion, hasMod, modVersion, hasClass, per-object ifNotMatch, and top-level conditionBehaivor: AND|OR, see Conditions & Packs → Conditions) is evaluated once per document, before validation or apply. A failing condition produces exactly one diagnostic: Skipped by conditions: Required mod 'SomeMod' is not loaded **This diagnostic is Info severity, and BuildReportString (the text behind /kdf report) explicitly skips every Info-severity entry before printing.** That's not a report-formatting quirk you can work around with a flag. The same filtered string is also what the in-game editor's load report scans for [Error]/[Warning] to decide whether to flag a problem, so a condition typo produces zero visible signal anywhere a player normally looks. The document is silently skipped, every single time, and neither /kdf report nor the in-game editor will ever mention it. There is currently no player-facing switch that surfaces Info diagnostics: no debug-log line, no /kdf report -v, nothing. The condition evaluator itself doesn't log anything either. It only ever returns a fail reason string that the framework then buries at Info severity. The only reliable way to catch this today is to **temporarily delete or comment out the document's conditions: block, save, and reload with /kdf reload or KDF.Reload, then inspect /kdf report.** If your document suddenly counts toward "document(s) applied" (or your op's debug line from Step 5 appears) with the block removed, the condition was the culprit. Put the block back, reload again, and check it against Conditions & Packs for exact key names, mod ref spelling, version-range syntax (gameVersion/hasMod/modVersion all use SML semver ranges), and array grouping (ifNotMatch negates only its containing object), and conditionBehaivor spelling/ value (AND is default; conditionBehavior is accepted as an alias).

sections.heading: Step 4: did the document validate?
sections.text: Every handler runs ValidateDocument before ApplyDocument. The two check fundamentally different things. - ValidateDocument is structural. Is the document even shaped correctly? Missing required keys, wrong node kind (map vs. sequence), or malformed op entries would all fail here. This runs purely against the parsed YAML, so it never touches the live game and can't fail because a class doesn't exist. Failures here are Error-severity and often carry a real line number (Entry->Line), because they're about one specific YAML node. Example, from type: cdo: [Error] my-pack/bad.cdo.yml:12: 'matchTag', 'matchName' and 'where' require an 'ofClass' scope class (only the recipe shortcuts 'producedIn', 'ingredient', 'product' default to FGRecipe) If ValidateDocument returns false, ApplyDocument is never called for that document. It's zero ops, and the document doesn't count toward "document(s) applied" in the report at all. - ApplyDocument is semantic. Now it resolves your YAML against the actual running game. Does target: point at a real, loadable class or object? Does matchTag / producedIn / where + ofClass match anything? This is where a structurally-perfect document can still fail because a path is wrong or a class doesn't exist: [Error] my-pack/bad.cdo.yml: Target '/Game/Typo/Path.Path_C' is neither a loadable class nor object (...) Critically, these failures are per patch entry, not per document. One bad target: inside a document with several patch entries only skips that entry. The rest still apply, and the document still counts as applied as long as at least one entry succeeded. So an Error with a line number pointing at your YAML structure means Step 4a: fix the shape. An Error naming an unresolved path/class means Step 4b: fix the reference, or check spelling and the _C suffix (see Targeting → Choosing a selector).

sections.heading: Step 5: did the specific op apply?
sections.text: If you've gotten this far (the file is found, the type resolved, conditions passed, and the document validated and applied with no errors) but the _specific value you expected to change_ still looks vanilla, turn on debug logging: - Per document: debug: true at the top level of the file. - Per pack: debug: true in pack.yml. - Global: console variable KDF.Debug 1 (or launch with -KDFDebug), or /kdf debug on from chat. This also logs ops originating from the in-game editor. With logging enabled, run /kdf reload or KDF.Reload, then /kdf report to inspect the new pass. Every successfully applied op logs exactly one line at Log verbosity from FKDFPatchUtil::LogAppliedOp: [KDF DEBUG] <file>: <target>.<property> <op> : <pre> -> <post> For example: [KDF DEBUG] faster-smelting.cdo.yml: /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C.mManufactoringDuration multiply : 2.000000 -> 1.000000 There are two outcomes here. - Your op's line never appears at all: it never reached the apply step. That means one of Steps 1 to 4 above is still the real problem. Most often the property path silently resolved to a _different_ object than you expected, or the op failed and produced an Error you missed in /kdf report. A failed op logs nothing here; it only ever logs on success. - Your op's line appears, but the pre/post values aren't what you assumed: the pipeline worked exactly as written. Your assumption about which property holds the value (or its starting value) was wrong. Compare <pre> against what you expected the vanilla value to be before writing more YAML. The log lives at %LOCALAPPDATA%\FactoryGame\Saved\Logs\FactoryGame.log in a packaged game. Search for [KDF DEBUG].

sections.heading: Step 6: did you reload the saved changes?
sections.text: KDataForge first loads at GameInstance INITIALIZATION. After that load completes, save the file, run /kdf reload as the host or a dedicated-server administrator, or use KDF.Reload in the host/server console. Then inspect /kdf report. Reload restores captured property baselines, rescans YAML, and reruns the apply stages; check its summary for baseline-restore warnings too. Reload affects only the host/server process where it runs. It does not update connected clients. Restart the session for frozen content registrations, irreversible world changes, and data explicitly documented as cold or restart-bound.

sections.heading: Quick reference
sections.text: | Step | Question | What to check | | 1: Scanning | Did the pack/document count in /kdf report change at all? | Root marker (DataForge, data-editor, or direct pack.yml), depth ≤ 6 from the project root, not nested inside a pruned directory, file extension .yml/.yaml | | 2: Type resolution | Is there a [Warning] about no type / no handler for the type? | type: key spelling, <name>.<type>.yml filename convention, typo in a known type name (remember: the "no handler" warning is deduped to one per type, not one per file) | | 3: Conditions | Does the document have a conditions: block at all? | Temporarily comment it out, save, reload, then run /kdf report. If the document applies, check the condition. Restore the block and reload again. Condition-skips are Info-severity and filtered out of the report | | 4: Validation/Apply | Is there an [Error] in /kdf report, with or without a line number? | Line number present means structural (ValidateDocument), fix the YAML shape. No line number, naming a path/class, means semantic (ApplyDocument), fix the reference | | 5: Op-level apply | Turn on debug: true / KDF.Debug 1. Does your op's [KDF DEBUG] line appear? | Missing entirely means it never reached apply, back to Steps 1 to 4. Present but wrong pre/post means a property/assumption issue, not a pipeline bug | | 6: Reload scope | Did you reload after saving YAML? | Host/server: /kdf reload or KDF.Reload, then /kdf report. Reload is process-local. Restart for frozen registrations, irreversible world changes, or explicitly cold/restart-bound data | Create your first pack: trace an operation covers all three debug switches and the log location. Its load and verification step defines the Info, Warning, and Error levels used here. Diagnostics, never failures explains why a skipped patch entry never halts the rest of the load.

pages.title: Edit another mod's data assets
pages.description: Rebalancing existing KAPI or RefinedR&D data asset instances without creating a new one and without a hard dependency on the mod that owns them.

sections.heading: Edit another mod's data assets
sections.text: Use a cdo patch with a conditions: gate to retune existing KAPI or RefinedR&D data assets (RefinedPower or FicsitFarming). The gate lets the pack skip cleanly when the owning mod is not installed. You do not need a special document type.

sections.heading: Data assets use normal `cdo` patches
sections.text: UDataAsset instances are objects sitting in memory just like a recipe or schematic CDO. KAPI and many RefinedR&D assets derive from UPrimaryDataAsset, which matters for consumer discovery, but KDataForge edits both primary and plain data assets with the exact same type: cdo document, the same properties: op grammar, and the same target:/allAssetsOfClass:/matchTag: selectors used everywhere else in this framework. There's no "data asset patch" document. type: dataasset is a different, narrower tool. It only creates a brand-new instance (package /KDataForge/GenAssets/<PackRef>, announced to the asset registry). Once that instance exists, whether type: dataasset made it or the target mod shipped it, you tune it exactly like this tutorial shows. See Data Assets → Creating new instances if you want to create one from scratch instead. One more contrast is worth keeping in mind. Schematics need register: false when you reach into one you don't own (see Adding a Recipe to an Existing Schematic), because register-only mode still touches SML's content registry. Plain cdo patches on a data-asset instance never register anything. You're mutating an object that's already alive, so there's no register: flag to think about here at all.

sections.heading: Three ways to target an instance, and which to reach for
sections.text: Data Assets → Editing KAPI data assets and Targeting document all three selectors in full; here's the practical decision for data-asset instances specifically: | Selector | Use it when… | Trade-off | | target: object path (no _C) | You know exactly which instance, for example only the Iron miner description | Fastest and most precise, but you need the exact path. Get it from /kdf editor (browse the asset) or the asset registry. It can change if the owning mod renames the asset | | allAssetsOfClass: | You want every instance of a type retuned the same way, for example every KAPI cleaner recipe or every RefinedR&D boiler | The usual default for rebalancing a whole machine family. No path-hunting needed | | matchTag: + ofClass: | You want a subset, for example only the event-tagged miner descriptions | Needs the target assets to actually carry a matching tag. KAPI assets implement IGameplayTagAssetInterface, so mTags matches directly with no tagProperty: override needed | For a first pass at rebalancing a whole mod's assets, allAssetsOfClass: is almost always the right starting point. It's what the worked scenario below uses for both mods.

sections.heading: Worked scenario: bulk-tune two mods, neither as a hard dependency
sections.text: Say you want two independent tweaks. KAPI's modular miners should produce fluid a bit faster, and every RefinedR&D boiler (RefinedPower's, FicsitFarming's, or anyone else's built on RefinedRDApi) should cook faster too. Neither mod is a dependency of your pack. A conditions: block with hasMod: gates each document so it's a clean skip, not a hard error, if that mod isn't loaded. # file: kapi-miner-fluid-tuning.cdo.yml type: cdo conditions: hasMod: KAPI patches: - allAssetsOfClass: /Script/KAPI.KAPIModularMinerDescription properties: mNormalFluidCountPerSecond: $op: multiply value: 1.25 # file: refinedrd-boiler-tuning.cdo.yml type: cdo conditions: hasMod: RefinedRDApi patches: - allAssetsOfClass: /Script/RefinedRDApi.RRDABoilerDataAsset properties: mDuration: $op: multiply value: 0.85 These are two separate documents, not one. conditions: gates the whole document, and these two tweaks depend on two different mods being present, so they can't share a file.

sections.heading: Automatic consumer rescans
sections.text: KAPI and RefinedRDApi cache asset scans. After KDataForge's initial document load, it rescans an installed consumer only when data assets changed: - KAPI's StartScanForDataAssets is resolved and called through reflection when KAPI is loaded. - RefinedRDApi's equivalent method is resolved the same way. KDataForge has no link or plugin dependency on either mod. Keep hasMod: on a YAML document so class references are skipped cleanly when their owner is absent.

sections.heading: The key-field crash gotcha
sections.text: A handful of properties on KAPI assets are load-bearing enough that the game **intentionally crashes** if you null them out. Examples include mResourceClass on miner descriptions, mInFluid.ItemClass on cleaner items, and mWidgetClass on tooltip injectors. This tutorial won't repeat the full list; see Data Assets → key-field warning before you write a set op against any of these. If your goal is "turn this instance off," use mIsDisabled: true instead. Every KAPI asset has it, and it's exactly what it's for.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - The patch silently does nothing: check the exact spelling of your hasMod: value (KAPI, RefinedRDApi, case matters) and confirm through /kdf report that the target mod is loaded. A failed conditions: check shows up there as an Info diagnostic, not an error. A search for errors alone will miss it. - allAssetsOfClass: matches zero assets: double-check the exact class path (/Script/KAPI.KAPIModularMinerDescription, /Script/RefinedRDApi.RRDABoilerDataAsset, etc.). A typo'd module or class name matches nothing rather than erroring. /kdf report lists every asset a selector matched, so you can confirm the count before you trust the values it set. - Values look patched in the report but the in-game behaviour didn't change: check whether the property you touched is one KAPI/RRDA only reads once at scan time, versus one read live every tick. If it's the former, confirm the automatic rescan ran after the initial load. If it still looks stale, the more likely cause is a second document overriding the same property later in load order. This guide builds on the full KAPI and RRDA property reference in Data Assets and the selector details in Targeting. For the equivalent "I do not own this, I am extending it" pattern with schematics, see Adding a Recipe to an Existing Schematic.

pages.title: Add a recipe to an existing schematic
pages.description: Unlocking a new or existing recipe from a schematic you didn't generate (vanilla, another mod's, or your own from an earlier pack), with either a direct cdo append or the schematic class shortcut.

sections.heading: Add a recipe to an existing schematic
sections.text: An existing schematic can be vanilla, owned by another mod, or generated by an earlier pack version. To make it unlock another recipe, use a direct cdo append for the smallest patch or use type: schematic with class: for the same syntax as a generated schematic.

sections.heading: Direct fix: `type: cdo` append to `mUnlocks`
sections.text: mUnlocks is an instanced UObject array. For append, prepend, insert, or set, KDataForge can construct each new entry from a class: plus nested properties: block before adding it to the array. # file: append-extra-recipe.cdo.yml type: cdo patches: - target: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-2.Schematic_1-2_C properties: mUnlocks: $op: append value: class: /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties: mRecipes: - /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_Recipe_MyNewRecipe Use a sequence under value: if you want to append several unlock objects in one operation.

sections.heading: Schematic shortcut: `type: schematic` with `class:`
sections.text: # file: unlock-extra-recipe.schematic.yml type: schematic schematics: - class: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Progression/Schematic_1-2.Schematic_1-2_C # the EXISTING schematic register: false # it's already registered by the base game don't re-register it unlocks: - class: /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties: mRecipes: - /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_Recipe_MyNewRecipe - class: (instead of id:) tells KDataForge "don't generate a class, resolve this existing one". See Type: recipe → register-only mode for the general id:/class: duality, since schematics work the same way. - unlocks: applies even in register-only mode. The schematic content-creation handler runs properties: and unlocks: against whatever CDO it resolved, whether that CDO came from generating a new class or from resolving an existing one. This is the one detail that makes the whole pattern work. - register: false matters here. register: true (the default) is right when the schematic is _yours_ and this is the first time anything registers it. For a vanilla schematic, or one another mod already registers, it's already known to UModContentRegistry. You're only reaching into its CDO to add an extra unlock, not re-announcing its existence. Set register: false to avoid registering it a second time under your mod's reference.

sections.heading: Use the same pattern for your own existing schematic
sections.text: Nothing changes if the schematic is one you generated in an earlier pack version. Just point class: at its generated path instead of a vanilla one, and leave register: false for the same reason: it's already registered from whichever document first created and registered it. type: schematic schematics: - class: /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_Schematic_SuperIngot register: false unlocks: - class: /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties: mRecipes: - /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_Recipe_PureSuperIngot

sections.heading: Unlocking something other than a recipe
sections.text: The same class: + unlocks: shape works for any concrete FGUnlock subclass. Supported classes include FGUnlockRecipe, inventory slots, schematics that unlock other schematics, custom unlock types from other mods, and anything else you'd normally put in a schematic's unlocks: list at generation time. See Type: schematic → Instanced unlocks for the full list of what an unlock entry can configure.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - "class: could not be resolved": double check the exact path, including the _C suffix for Blueprint schematics. The bare class-name shortcut also works here (see Targeting → bare class name) if you only know the short name. - **The recipe registers but the schematic seems to unlock it twice, or you see a warning about duplicate registration**: you likely left register: true (the default) on a schematic that's already registered elsewhere. Add register: false. - This is for adding an unlock to something that already exists. For building a brand new schematic from scratch, see Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock instead. The Type: schematic reference covers mType, unlocks:, and generate-versus-register behavior. Type: recipe uses the same id: and class: duality one stage earlier. For the full new-content chain, see Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock.

pages.title: From live edits to a shareable pack
pages.description: Test a change in the in-game editor, move it into the Packs workspace, and verify the saved YAML.

sections.heading: From live edits to a shareable pack
sections.text: /kdf editor has two workspaces. Runtime inspects loaded objects and applies property edits to the current process. Packs creates and edits YAML files on disk. A live edit lasts only for the current session, while a saved pack can be reloaded, restarted, versioned, and distributed. This guide retunes a recipe in Runtime, exports the change, and places it in a pack created through the Packs workspace.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text: You need a running game with KDataForge and a recipe you can test. In multiplayer, use the same pack files on the host or dedicated server and every client. KDataForge does not transfer files or live editor operations between processes. Open the editor with /kdf editor. The top toolbar switches between Runtime and Packs.

sections.heading: Test the change in Runtime
sections.text: 1. Select Runtime. 2. Choose Recipes, then search for the recipe you want to change. 3. Select the recipe and find mManufactoringDuration in the inspector. 4. Commit a new value. The editor applies the change through the same operation pipeline used by YAML patches. 5. Craft the recipe and check its duration. Runtime keeps an undo and redo history for the current session. The side panel also shows YAML, the recorded diff, references, and applied operations for the selected object.

sections.heading: Export the tested change
sections.text: Use Export Diff for a focused patch. When the selected object has active live-editor operations, the export writes those operations with their arguments. If it has none, the handler falls back to the top-level properties that received a first-write snapshot in the current session. An earlier YAML operation can create such a snapshot. Opening a property without writing it does not. Export Full writes every reflected property that is not deprecated, transient, or editor-only. This can freeze unrelated defaults at their current values, so use it only when you intend to own the full reflected state. 1. Keep the edited recipe selected. 2. Select Export Diff. 3. Read the status line for the written path. The editor creates the destination directory when needed and writes: <ProjectDir>/DataForge/exported/<ObjectName>.cdo.yml For a class default object, <ObjectName> is usually an Unreal name such as Default__Recipe_IngotIron_C. The filename does not determine the target. The YAML inside the file contains the target path. A one-property export looks like this: type: cdo patches: - target: /KDataForge/Gen/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_Recipe_SuperIngot properties: mManufactoringDuration: 2.0 The editor writes operation arguments under $op: properties: mManufactoringDuration: $op: multiply value: 2 If you change the same property more than once, the export writes successive patches so both operations keep their order. A literal value map containing $op is exported with $op: set and the literal map nested under value: to distinguish it from an operation.

sections.heading: Create the destination pack
sections.text: 1. Switch to Packs. 2. Under New Pack, enter a name containing letters, numbers, _, or -. 3. Select Create. The editor creates this folder and manifest: <ProjectDir>/Mods/DataForge/<pack-name>/ pack.yml The manifest starts with a stable ref, the same display name, version 1.0.0, a placeholder description, priority 100, enabled: true, and debug: false. Edit the description and version before distribution. Treat ref as permanent after players have used generated content from the pack. If you already have a pack, select it in Pack Browser instead of creating another one.

sections.heading: Put the export in the pack
sections.text: You can move the exported .cdo.yml file into the new pack directory with a file manager. Select Refresh in Pack Browser after moving it. You can also create the destination file in the editor: 1. Select the pack in Pack Browser. 2. Under New Document, choose cdo. 3. Enter a filename without an extension and select Create document. The editor adds .cdo.yml automatically. 4. Open the exported file in a text editor and copy its YAML. 5. In KDataForge, select Raw YAML and replace the generated skeleton with the exported YAML. 6. Switch to Form. The editor parses the raw text before opening the form. Invalid YAML keeps you in Raw YAML and reports the parse error. 7. Select Save. Save validates the YAML and replaces the file on disk. If the replacement fails, the original file is preserved. The status line gives the exact path and reminds you to run /kdf reload.

sections.heading: Edit pack files in Form or Raw YAML
sections.text: The Form view exposes the parsed YAML tree. Select a node to replace it, add a child, remove it, or use contextual suggestions for fields, classes, properties, and known values. The form preserves handler-supported values that do not have a specialized control as raw YAML nodes. For a new empty properties: map, select that node and use Choose field or + Field / entry to add a reflected property as a key. A struct value can be expanded as a nested map and filled with its reflected fields. To apply an operation, put $op: multiply and value: 2 on separate lines beneath the numeric property key. Select $op to choose a supported operation from Known value. Existing properties: operation lists remain editable. Use Raw YAML for multi-document files, larger edits, or direct pasting. Switching back to Form parses the current text and synchronizes the tree. Save always parses again before writing. The editor tracks unsaved changes to the open file: - Save writes them to disk. - Revert reloads the selected file and discards the unsaved version. - Switching to another pack or file is blocked until you save or revert. - Creating another pack or document is also blocked while the current file is dirty. - Closing the editor from the Packs workspace shows a warning with Cancel and Discard and close. Refresh updates Pack Browser after files were added or moved outside the editor. It is not a replacement for Save or Revert.

sections.heading: Apply and verify the saved pack
sections.text: 1. Run /kdf reload as the host or a dedicated-server administrator. 2. Run /kdf report and confirm that the pack and document loaded without an Error. 3. Test the recipe again. 4. Restart the session if the report or feature page marks the change as cold, frozen, or restart-bound. Reload restores captured property baselines, rescans the files, and reapplies the current pack set in that process. Frozen content registrations, irreversible world changes, and packs using native CDO helpers still require a restart.

sections.heading: Create new documents directly in Packs
sections.text: The Packs workspace can create typed documents for CDO patches, gameplay tags, assets, localization, generated classes and content, data assets, curves, sink points, resource nodes, sublevels, sounds, and pack configuration. Each new file gets the correct <name>.<type>.yml suffix and a valid starting shape for that type. This is the preferred editor workflow for new pack files. Follow the relevant feature page to fill the generated document because a valid skeleton does not contain the gameplay data for a finished item, recipe, schematic, or world rule.

sections.heading: Runtime Create drafts
sections.text: Runtime also retains a Create panel for drafting an item, resource, building, recipe, schematic, research tree, unlock, data asset, or generic class from a loaded parent. It writes the selected parent's current reflected values to: <ProjectDir>/DataForge/created/<Id>.<Kind>.yml The draft uses property names as mapping keys, including nested struct maps and instanced-object properties: maps. Review the values and references before adding the file to a pack. The editor creates the created directory when needed. This action writes a draft and does not apply the new content to the running session. Move the reviewed draft into a named pack and restart when its content registration requires it. For new work, the Packs workspace usually avoids this extra staging step.

sections.heading: Export Diff contains little or nothing
sections.text: Diff includes properties written on the selected object during the current session. Confirm that you committed the value and still have the same object selected. Browsing a row does not record a snapshot.

sections.heading: An undone property still appears in Export Diff
sections.text: Undo removes its live operation. The first-write snapshot remains, so after you undo every active operation the fallback export can still include the current top-level property value. Review the YAML and remove a no-op property before publishing if you do not want the pack to own it.

sections.heading: Export Full contains internal-looking fields
sections.text: Full export includes reflected fields even when Unreal does not mark them as normally editable. It excludes deprecated, transient, and editor-only fields. Review the output and prefer Diff for a small balance patch.

sections.heading: Form will not open
sections.text: Raw YAML contains a parse error or a document root that is not a map. Read the status line, correct the raw text, then switch to Form again. You can use the linter for schema checks beyond parsing.

sections.heading: A saved change has no effect
sections.text: Save writes the file but does not apply it. Run /kdf reload, inspect /kdf report, and follow any restart rule for the affected document or property. A generated content draft may require a restart because the game registry has already frozen its session state.

sections.heading: Another player does not see the change
sections.text: Live edits and reloads are process-local. Copy the saved pack to every multiplayer process and use the same version on the server, host, and clients. Getting started covers pack discovery and reporting. Targeting explains selectors and spawned-actor patches. The separate UE Editor integration applies YAML to Unreal Editor assets with KDF.ApplyToAssets; it is not the in-game /kdf editor workflow.

pages.title: Item, icon, recipe, and Tier 1 unlock
pages.description: The most common first pack, a new item with a placeholder icon, a recipe that produces it, and a Tier-1 schematic that actually makes it obtainable in a fresh game.

sections.heading: Item, icon, recipe, and Tier 1 unlock
sections.text: This tutorial builds the minimum complete chain for an obtainable item: item, icon, recipe, and schematic. Each snippet is a complete working example.

sections.heading: The mistake this tutorial fixes
sections.text: A generated item and a recipe producing it are not enough on their own. Recipe: documents register the recipe class into SML's UModContentRegistry, so the game knows the class exists. Registration alone doesn't put the recipe in front of the player, though. Satisfactory gates every recipe behind an unlock, normally granted by a schematic (a HUB milestone or a MAM node). Without a schematic unlocking your recipe, the class exists and the recipe is "known" to the mod content registry, but the player still never sees it. That's the whole story behind "I don't see my created item."

sections.heading: Step 1: the item
sections.text: # file: super-ingot.item.yml type: item items: - id: SuperIngot parent: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties: mDisplayName: key: SuperIngot_Name ns: KDFSample source: Super Ingot mDescription: Forged from YAML. Stacks high, sinks well. mStackSize: SS_HUGE mResourceSinkPoints: 42 # Placeholder icon see Step 2, loaded by super-ingot-icon.asset.yml mSmallIcon: /KDataForge/GenAssets/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_SuperIngotIcon mPersistentBigIcon: /KDataForge/GenAssets/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_SuperIngotIcon mStackSize is an EStackSize enum (SS_ONE/SS_SMALL/SS_MEDIUM/SS_BIG/SS_HUGE/ SS_FLUID), not a plain item count. See Balancing → Items for the full caveat about the engine's stack-size cache. KDataForge refreshes that cache automatically, so you don't need to do anything extra. Just don't write a raw number here expecting it to mean "N items per stack".

sections.heading: Step 2: a placeholder icon (`type: asset`)
sections.text: You don't need real art to get an item on-screen and testable. Any PNG/JPG/TGA/BMP works, even your mod's own logo, as a stand-in until you have real icons: # file: super-ingot-icon.asset.yml type: asset assets: - id: SuperIngotIcon file: mod-logo.png # pack-relative path any 2D image Result: /KDataForge/GenAssets/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_SuperIngotIcon, referenced directly from the item's mSmallIcon/mPersistentBigIcon in Step 1. No include: needed. type: asset always runs in the Assets stage, and Assets always runs before Items, regardless of file or pack order. See Data Assets for the full type: asset reference. This is the same 2D-image mechanism, just used for an item icon instead of a KAPI data asset.

sections.heading: Step 3: the recipe
sections.text: # file: super-ingot.recipe.yml type: recipe recipes: - id: Recipe_SuperIngot properties: mDisplayName: 'Super Ingot' mIngredients: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C Amount: 2 mProduct: - ItemClass: /KDataForge/Gen/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_SuperIngot Amount: 1 mManufactoringDuration: 4.0 mProducedIn: - /Game/FactoryGame/Buildable/Factory/SmelterMk1/Build_SmelterMk1.Build_SmelterMk1_C No include: needed for the item reference. Items always finishes before Recipes starts. This alone gets you a real, registered recipe class, but it's still locked.

sections.heading: Step 4: the Tier-1 schematic (the step that was missing)
sections.text: # file: super-ingot.schematic.yml type: schematic schematics: - id: Schematic_SuperIngot properties: mType: EST_Milestone mDisplayName: Super Ingot Production mDescription: Unlocks production of the Super Ingot. mTechTier: 1 mTimeToComplete: 10 mCost: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C Amount: 20 unlocks: - class: /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties: mRecipes: - /KDataForge/Gen/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_Recipe_SuperIngot - mType: EST_Milestone + mTechTier: 1 is what makes this a Tier 1 HUB milestone: the standard "unlocked early, no MAM required" pattern. - No include: needed. Recipes always finishes before Schematics starts. - register: true is the default, so this schematic (and, via SML's auto-propagation, the recipe and item it touches) registers into UModContentRegistry automatically. The schematic is the only piece in this whole chain you need registration for. See Type: recipe → auto-propagation. With this file in place, a fresh save now shows "Super Ingot Production" as a purchasable Tier 1 HUB milestone. Purchasing it unlocks Recipe_SuperIngot for the player to build.

sections.heading: Recap: what each file contributes
sections.text: | File | type: | Contributes | | super-ingot.item.yml | item | The item class itself | | super-ingot-icon.asset.yml | asset | A 2D texture the item references as its icon | | super-ingot.recipe.yml | recipe | A recipe producing the item (registered, but locked) | | super-ingot.schematic.yml | schematic | The unlock: this is what makes it obtainable |

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Item still not appearing after adding the schematic: run /kdf report and confirm all four documents applied with no errors. A typo'd generated-class path (missing pack ref, wrong id spelling) is the most common cause, and it's always visible there. - Icon shows as a checkerboard/missing texture: check that file: is spelled exactly right and is relative to the pack root (the directory containing pack.yml), not the mod's own folder. - Recipe exists but isn't selectable at the smelter: the recipe needs the schematic's unlock applied. In a fresh save that means purchasing "Super Ingot Production" in the HUB. - Want to unlock a NEW recipe from a schematic that already exists (vanilla or another mod's, instead of generating your own): that's a slightly different shape, covered in Adding a Recipe to an Existing Schematic. For per-document details, use Type: item, Type: recipe, and Type: schematic. Data Assets documents the full type: asset 2D-image mechanism. End-to-End Pack shows a similar chain with localization and sink points.

pages.title: Localizing your pack
pages.description: Shipping new text in multiple languages, overriding existing vanilla or modded strings without retyping them, and iterating with translators live with session restarts, without breaking on the next game update.

sections.heading: Localizing your pack
sections.text: type: localization can add text for generated content or override an existing FactoryGame, mod, or earlier pack string. These jobs use different YAML shapes. This tutorial covers both forms, the one-file-per-culture layout for multiple languages, and the restart-based translation workflow.

sections.heading: The two entry forms
sections.text: Every entry under entries: is either a scalar or a block map with source and text fields, and UKDFLocalizationHandler treats them very differently. The scalar form, Key: "some text", registers a brand-new (namespace, key) pair. It sets both the source and the displayed text to the same string, and you use it for new text nobody has already registered. The map form, Key: with nested source: and text: fields, overrides an existing (namespace, key) pair instead. Here text: is what displays, while source: must match the target's current source string, and you use it for retexting something that already exists. Omitting source: in the map form makes the handler reuse text: as the source. That's just the scalar form written longer, and it only works for new keys. > ⚠️ The (namespace, key) an entry targets is exactly namespace: (document-level) plus the > entry's own key under entries:. Nothing is inferred. That pair, plus a hash of source:, > is what the engine checks before it will display your text:. Get either wrong and nothing > errors: you just get an unused row in the localization table that nothing ever reads.

sections.heading: Step 1: give your item a keyed display name
sections.text: Overriding _anything_ later requires the text to have a real (namespace, key) pair in the first place. A plain string mDisplayName is culture-invariant (see Property Types → FText: plain (culture-invariant)). Invariant text never goes through the localization system at all, so nothing you write under type: localization can ever touch it. Use the keyed map form instead, exactly like the sample pack's own Super Ingot: # file: super-ingot.item.yml (excerpt) type: item items: - id: SuperIngot properties: mDisplayName: key: SuperIngot_Name ns: KDFSample source: Super Ingot ns: KDFSample + key: SuperIngot_Name is now the address every translation for this item's name has to target.

sections.heading: Step 2: one file per culture
sections.text: Nothing forces you into a single translation file. The natural, idiomatic pattern is **one file per language**, all targeting the same namespace:/keys. For example, a German file: # file: super-ingot.localization.yml type: localization namespace: KDFSample culture: de entries: SuperIngot_Name: source: Super Ingot text: Superbarren Adding French is just another file with a different culture:. Nothing about the item, the namespace, or the key changes: # file: super-ingot-fr.localization.yml type: localization namespace: KDFSample culture: fr entries: SuperIngot_Name: source: Super Ingot text: Super Lingot Both files apply independently. culture: gates each one against the _currently running_ language, so shipping a dozen languages is a dozen small files, not one giant one. Nothing stops you from grouping several keys from several items into one per-culture file either, once your pack grows past a single item. The namespace/culture gate is per-document, not per-file.

sections.heading: Step 3: override existing text
sections.text: Overriding your own earlier text is trivial: you already know the exact namespace:/key, because you're the one who chose them in Step 1. Want to retcon the German name later without touching the item file? Add another entry with the map form, same namespace/key, same source: type: localization namespace: KDFSample culture: de entries: SuperIngot_Name: source: 'Super Ingot' text: 'Ur-Superbarren' **Overriding vanilla or another mod's text is the same mechanism. You just don't get to pick the namespace/key.** They belong to whatever FText the target already carries, and you have to go find them: - Use /kdf editor in a normal running game or in the UE editor. Browse to the target object (a vanilla schematic, another mod's item, anything KDataForge can resolve) and use Export. If mDisplayName exports as a map containing key, ns, and source, that map _is_ the real address. Copy it verbatim, keep key/ns/source identical, and only change text:. - Or read the source mod's own localization files directly. Most KMods ship Content/Localization/<Mod>/*.archive/.manifest alongside the plugin, which is a faster way to confirm a key than booting the game. - If Export shows a plain string instead of a map, the target is culture-invariant. Stop here: there is no (namespace, key) to attach an override to. The only way to change it is a plain cdo patch on the property itself (see Patching (type: cdo)), which replaces the text for every language at once, not per-culture. Worked example: a schematic whose author (you, an earlier pack version, or another mod) declared mDisplayName with the keyed form: # somewhere upstream the schematic's own properties: mDisplayName: key: Schematic_SuperIngot_Name ns: MyPack source: 'Super Ingot Production' # file: fr.localization.yml translating (or retexting) it without touching the schematic type: localization namespace: MyPack culture: fr entries: Schematic_SuperIngot_Name: source: 'Super Ingot Production' text: 'Production de Super Lingot' namespace: MyPack + Schematic_SuperIngot_Name has to match the schematic's declaration character-for-character, and source: has to match the _current_ source string byte-for-byte. Get either one wrong and this document applies cleanly, with no error, while the schematic keeps showing its untranslated name. > Recipes are a special case. FGRecipe::mDisplayName is only shown if the recipe's own > mDisplayNameOverride flag is true. Otherwise the UI shows the first product's item name > instead, and a recipe-name translation you write will never be visible no matter how correct it > is. If you want a recipe-specific name (and its translations) to appear, set > mDisplayNameOverride: true alongside mDisplayName in the recipe's own properties:. > Otherwise, translate the produced item's name instead.

sections.heading: Translation iteration workflow
sections.text: 1. Edit the .yml translation file. 2. Select the matching game language in the Options menu. 3. Restart the session and inspect /kdf report. culture: is evaluated against the language active during session initialization. A culture: fr document is intentionally skipped while the game runs in English.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - A translation applied but nothing changed in-game. This is almost always a source-hash mismatch: source: must be byte-identical to the text's _current_ stored source (spacing, punctuation, capitalisation), since it's a hash comparison, not a fuzzy match. If a game update changed the base string, every override keyed off the old one silently stops matching. Copy the string straight out of an /kdf editor Export, never retype it from memory. - My override document loads with no errors but the text is still untranslated. Check the namespace:/key pair against exactly what the target FText was declared with, not a name you invented. This is the difference between "new text" and "override": new keys can use any namespace/key you like, while overrides have to match the target's real ones exactly. - A whole culture file seems to be ignored. Look for a stray or misspelled culture: (e.g. de_DE instead of de-DE, or a typo like germna). The log line reads `skipped: culture <X> does not match current language <Y> when this happens. Omitting culture:` entirely applies to every language, which is usually what you want unless you're intentionally splitting per locale. - Overriding a recipe's display name does nothing. Check mDisplayNameOverride on that recipe: if it's false, the UI ignores mDisplayName entirely and shows the first product's item name. - Export shows a plain string, not a map containing key, ns, and source. The target text is culture-invariant, so no localization override will ever reach it. Change it with a cdo patch on the property instead (this affects every language, not one). - **Trying to cdo-patch a schematic/recipe/item you generated yourself, to convert its mDisplayName to the keyed form.** CDOChanges runs _before_ Items/Recipes/Schematics in the fixed stage order, so a cdo patch can't even resolve a KDataForge-generated class's path yet. Edit the generating document's own properties: block directly instead (item.yml/recipe.yml/ schematic.yml). There's no need for a separate patch for content you're already generating. Localization is the full reference for entry forms, culture matching, and source hashes. Property Types compares plain and keyed FText forms. Use Patching (type: cdo) for invariant text or properties that type: localization cannot reach. The Super Ingot used here comes from Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock.

pages.title: Player-Configurable Balancing
pages.description: Turn fixed pack numbers into settings players can change. Config fields, typed references, templates, config conditions, hot and cold values, and testing in single player and multiplayer.

sections.heading: Player-Configurable Balancing
sections.text: In this guide you give a pack five settings: how fast iron smelts, whether the output is doubled, which tier a milestone appears in, which tags a recipe carries, and a line of description text. You will see hot values change live and a cold value ask for a restart. The files are the configuration part of the KDFSample sample pack, so you can compare them with that pack. Read Pack Configuration first if you want the full rules behind each step. This page is the walkthrough.

sections.heading: What you will build
sections.text: Field Type Apply Used for balance.ironSpeed float slider 0.25 to 4 hot Divides the Iron Ingot smelting time features.enableBonus boolean hot Switches the doubled output on and off features.tier select ( int32 , 1 to 3) cold HUB tier of the Super Ingot milestone tags.extra list of gameplay tags hot Tags added to the Iron Ingot recipe texts.motto multiline text hot First sentence of the Super Ingot description

sections.heading: Step 1: the pack
sections.text: Create DataForge/pack.yml . description and icon are shown next to the pack in settings screens; the icon is a file in the pack folder. pack.yml ref : KDFSample name : KDataForge Sample Pack version : 1.0.0 description : Exercises pack configuration, templates and config conditions. icon : mod-logo.png

sections.heading: Step 2: the categories
sections.text: A settings screen groups fields by category and orders the groups by priority. Categories are ordinary generated classes whose parent is FGCategory . Create DataForge/sample-config-category.class.yml : sample-config-category.class.yml type : class classes : - id : SampleBalanceCategory parent : /Script/FactoryGame.FGCategory properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : SampleBalanceCategory_Name ns : KDFSample source : Sample Balance - path : mMenuPriority value : 10 - id : SampleFeaturesCategory parent : /Script/FactoryGame.FGCategory properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : SampleFeaturesCategory_Name ns : KDFSample source : Sample Features - path : mMenuPriority value : 20

sections.heading: Step 3: the config definition
sections.text: Create DataForge/kdf-sample.config.yml . The file name ending in .config.yml is what makes it a definition. category: at the top is the default; balance.ironSpeed overrides it. kdf-sample.config.yml type : config category : SampleFeaturesCategory fields : - id : balance.ironSpeed type : number valueType : float name : key : Config_IronSpeed_Name ns : KDFSample source : Iron smelting speed description : How many times faster the Iron Ingot recipe runs than in the base game. tooltip : title : Iron smelting speed text : 1 keeps the vanilla speed, 2 halves the smelting time, 4 is the maximum. category : SampleBalanceCategory default : 2 min : 0.25 max : 4 step : 0.25 decimals : 2 display : slider apply : hot - id : features.enableBonus type : boolean name : Double iron ingot output description : Doubles the amount of Iron Ingots one smelting cycle produces. default : true apply : hot - id : features.tier type : select valueType : int32 name : Super Ingot milestone tier description : HUB tier in which the Super Ingot Production milestone appears. default : 1 options : - value : 1 label : Tier 1 - value : 2 label : Tier 2 - value : 3 label : Tier 3 apply : cold - id : tags.extra type : text valueType : tag multiple : true tagRoot : KDF.Sample name : Extra recipe tags description : Gameplay tags that are added to the Iron Ingot recipe. default : - KDF.Sample.Test maxCount : 4 apply : hot - id : texts.motto type : text valueType : text multiline : true maxLength : 200 name : Super Ingot motto description : The first sentence of the Super Ingot description. default : Forged from YAML. Stacks high, sinks well. apply : hot Every field has a name , a description and (through the field or the document) a category. Start the game once. KDataForge creates FactoryGame/Configs/Packs/KDFSample.config.yml with the defaults.

sections.heading: Step 4: use a value in a patch
sections.text: Typed references replace a whole, unquoted scalar with the field’s typed value. Create DataForge/iron-ingot-faster.cdo.yml : iron-ingot-faster.cdo.yml type : cdo conditions : gameVersion : ' >=1.0.0 ' patches : - target : /Game/FactoryGame/Recipes/Smelter/Recipe_IngotIron.Recipe_IngotIron_C properties : # 1. Typed reference: the number 2.0 by default - path : mManufactoringDuration op : divide value : cfg:balance.ironSpeed # 2. Element condition: this operation exists only while the bonus is on - path : mProduct[0].Amount op : multiply value : 2 conditions : config : ' features.enableBonus ' # 3. A list field becomes a list of tags - path : mGameplayTags op : append value : cfg:tags.extra The three operations use all three ways to read a value: cfg:balance.ironSpeed fills the value: with the number. Because the slider’s minimum is 0.25, the division never hits zero. conditions: { config: ... } on the second operation takes the operation out of the list while features.enableBonus is off. It is an element condition and works on any entry of any list. cfg:tags.extra is a list field, so the reference becomes a list.

sections.heading: Step 5: use a value inside text
sections.text: Templates put values into strings. A string that starts with { has to be quoted. Create DataForge/super-ingot.item.yml : super-ingot.item.yml type : item items : - id : SuperIngot parent : /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties : - path : mDisplayName value : key : SuperIngot_Name ns : KDFSample source : Super Ingot - path : mDescription value : ' {cfg:texts.motto} Smelts like {item:/Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C:GetItemName} at {cfg:balance.ironSpeed}x speed. ' - path : mStackSize value : SS_HUGE With the defaults the description reads: Forged from YAML. Stacks high, sinks well. Smelts like Iron Ingot at 2.0x speed. {cfg:texts.motto} and {cfg:balance.ironSpeed} are replaced before anything is applied. {item:<class>:GetItemName} is read from the game when the property is written: the item provider calls the engine function GetItemName on the Iron Ingot class and returns the localized name. See Templates .

sections.heading: Step 6: a cold value
sections.text: The milestone’s tier is read when the game registers the schematic, so it is a cold value. In the schematic document the tier property takes the field like any other value: properties : - path : mTechTier value : cfg:features.tier features.tier has apply: cold , which is also the default. Changing it in the values file changes the saved value immediately, but the running game keeps the tier it started with and reports restart required .

sections.heading: Step 7: test it
sections.text: Load a save and open the chat. /kdf config dump KDFSample The fields are listed in no particular order, one line each, with the value, the default and the effective value: KDFSample:balance.ironSpeed [hot] = 2.0 (default 2.0, effective 2.0) KDFSample:features.enableBonus [hot] = true (default true, effective true) KDFSample:features.tier [cold] = 1 (default 1, effective 1) KDFSample:tags.extra [hot] = [KDF.Sample.Test] (default [KDF.Sample.Test], effective [KDF.Sample.Test]) KDFSample:texts.motto [hot] = Forged from YAML. Stacks high, sinks well. (default Forged from YAML. Stacks high, sinks well., effective Forged from YAML. Stacks high, sinks well.) 5 configuration field(s) Change a hot value and apply it: /kdf config set KDFSample:balance.ironSpeed 3 /kdf config apply KDFSample The reply says Saved: yes, reloaded: yes and lists the changed key. The Iron Ingot recipe now takes a third of its original time, and the Super Ingot description shows 3.0x . Turn the bonus off the same way ( /kdf config set KDFSample:features.enableBonus false ) and the recipe’s output returns to normal after the apply, because the element condition removed the operation. Now the cold value: /kdf config set KDFSample:features.tier 2 /kdf config apply KDFSample The reply ends with Restart required: KDFSample:features.tier (in yellow). The file now says tier: 2 , and /kdf config dump shows the value 2, restart required , and an effective value that is still 1. After the next start the milestone sits in tier 2. You can also edit FactoryGame/Configs/Packs/KDFSample.config.yml with a text editor and run /kdf reload : hot values apply, cold values report restart required. To try templates and expressions without touching any file: KDF.Template "{cfg:texts.motto} x{cfg:balance.ironSpeed}" KDFSample KDF.Config.Expr "features.enableBonus && balance.ironSpeed >= 2" KDFSample

sections.heading: Step 8: validate in the editor
sections.text: Open the project in the VS Code extension, or run kdf lint on the folder that contains DataForge/ . The editor checks the definition (required name and description , ids, ranges, defaults, categories), every cfg: reference and config: expression, template syntax, and whether a hot value feeds a cold place. Try breaking something: Edit Diagnostic cfg:balance.ironSped config.unknown-id config: !features.enableBonus config.expression-quote value: {cfg:texts.motto} text template.unquoted-start remove description from a field schema.required icon: nope.png pack.icon-missing See Lint Your Pack and the VS Code extension .

sections.heading: Step 9: let players change it in game
sections.text: Players can use the chat commands above, or edit the file. For a real settings screen, build a widget with the Blueprint Config API : list the packs with Get All Pack Infos , the fields with Get Config Descriptions Flat , create a slider, a checkbox, a dropdown and a text box per Get Kind , and call Apply Config Changes from an Apply button. The reference describes the full node flow.

sections.heading: Multiplayer
sections.text: On a listen server , the host changes values and they are sent to the clients while connected. Clients cannot edit them. On a dedicated server , edit the server’s values file and run /kdf reload , or change values as an administrator from a settings screen or with /kdf config set and /kdf config apply . A client whose cold features.tier differs from the host’s keeps its loaded content, reports a host mismatch, and can adopt the host’s values from the UI. A client never writes the host’s values to its own file, and leaving the session restores the local values. All players still need the same packs installed. See Pack Configuration .

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Symptom Fix /kdf config dump lists 0 fields The *.config.yml file is outside the pack, or a field has an error. Run /kdf report . The recipe did not change after apply The field is cold (restart), or the patch target is wrong. Check apply: hot and /kdf report . The description still shows {cfg:texts.motto} The scalar was not quoted, or the id is misspelled. A pre-pass token that cannot be resolved stays as written and logs a warning. Restart advised after applying a hot value The hot field also feeds a cold place. Use a cold field there, or restart. The category shows as FGCategory The category class was not found. Check the id in category: and that the .class.yml is in the same pack.

sections.heading: Where to go next
sections.text: Templates and Typed References : all providers, function calls, nesting and escaping Config Expressions : the full config: grammar Blueprint Config API : build the settings screen Conditions & Packs : where config: conditions can go

pages.title: Renaming content safely
pages.description: What you can rename in a pack for free, what needs a redirects entry, and the one rename redirects genuinely can't fix.

sections.heading: Renaming content safely
sections.text: A shipped pack can rename a file, a generated content id, or its pack ref. Each affects saved content differently. This guide explains all three cases and includes a complete before-and-after example for the supported redirect workflow.

sections.heading: The three renames
sections.text: | What you rename | Changes the generated class path? | Safe by default? | Fix | | A file (super-ingot.item.yml → ingot.item.yml) | No | Yes, always | Nothing: the filename is never part of any generated identity | | An id (id: MyItem → id: MyItemV2) | Yes | No | Add a redirects: entry in pack.yml (see below) | | A pack's ref | Yes, for _every_ id in the pack | No, and there's no fix | Don't. See "Renaming the pack ref" below | Generated classes live at /KDataForge/Gen/<PackRef> and are named Gen_<PackRef>_<Id>. This naming is deterministic and built from PackRef + id, never from a file path (Generated class identity). That's why the file is free and the other two aren't: the file was never part of the identity to begin with.

sections.heading: How `redirects:` works
sections.text: Syntax, in pack.yml: ref: MyPack version: 2.0.0 redirects: OldId: NewId # OldId: NewId, one entry per renamed id Under the hood (FKDFDynamicContentRegistry::ApplyRedirects in Source/KDataForge/Private/Content/KDFDynamicContent.cpp), each entry becomes one FCoreRedirect built from the pack's current ref: const FString OldPath = MakeClassPackageName(PackRef) + TEXT(".") + MakeClassName(PackRef, Redirect.Key); const FString NewPath = MakeClassPackageName(PackRef) + TEXT(".") + MakeClassName(PackRef, Redirect.Value); Redirects.Emplace(ECoreRedirectFlags::Type_Class, OldPath, NewPath); So a MyPack redirect MySuperIngot: SuperIngotMk2 registers a Type_Class redirect from /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_MySuperIngot to /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_SuperIngotMk2 via FCoreRedirects::AddRedirectList. When an old save deserialises a reference to the old class path, the engine's own class-path resolution walks through FCoreRedirects first and lands on the new class instead. The object loads normally, with no missing-class warning. It has to ship in the same version bump as the rename. ApplyRedirects runs once per pack ref, every session, right before any generated class can be referenced (UKDFSubsystem::ApplyStages, guarded by mRedirectedPacks so a live a session restart doesn't re-register it). There's nothing baked into the save. The redirect is re-derived from pack.yml on every load. That has one important consequence: if you ever delete the redirects: entry in a later version, the redirect stops being registered on the very next launch, and any save that still references the old class path breaks again. There's no expiry or "safe after N versions" in the code. Keep the entry in redirects: for as long as you want to support saves made before the rename. In practice that means indefinitely, unless you're certain every player has re-saved since.

sections.heading: Worked scenario: `MySuperIngot` → `SuperIngotMk2` in v2.0.0
sections.text: Before (pack version 1.0.0), generates /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_MySuperIngot: # file: super-ingot.item.yml type: item items: - id: MySuperIngot parent: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties: mDisplayName: Super Ingot After: rename the id, bump pack.yml, and add the redirect in the same version: # file: super-ingot.item.yml type: item items: - id: SuperIngotMk2 # renamed parent: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronIngot/Desc_IronIngot.Desc_IronIngot_C properties: mDisplayName: Super Ingot # file: pack.yml ref: MyPack name: My Content Pack version: 2.0.0 redirects: MySuperIngot: SuperIngotMk2 # OldId: NewId The class is now generated as /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_SuperIngotMk2. Any reference elsewhere in your own YAML (recipes, schematics, sink points) needs updating to the new path too. redirects: only fixes resolution of old save data: it doesn't rewrite your other documents for you. Any save made under v1.0.0 that still has Gen_MyPack_MySuperIngot embedded resolves straight through to Gen_MyPack_SuperIngotMk2 on load, with no warning. A second worked copy of this exact scenario also lives in End-to-End Pack → Renaming an id later if you want to see it next to a full multi-file pack.

sections.heading: Renaming the pack `ref`
sections.text: Don't. This is the one case where the honest answer is "unsupported," not "here's the workaround." ApplyRedirects takes a single PackRef and builds both the old and new class paths from it: MakeClassPackageName(PackRef) is the same call for OldPath and NewPath. There is no code path that builds an old path from one ref and a new path from a different ref. Since a ref rename changes /KDataForge/Gen/<PackRef> for every single generated class in the pack simultaneously, there's no mechanism, redirects: or otherwise, that bridges an old ref's package to a new ref's package. Every id in the pack would need its own cross-package redirect, and the feature does not build one. Treat ref: as permanent once you've shipped a version with real players. If you genuinely need a different display name, change name: instead. ref: is the save-persistence contract, and name: is cosmetic.

sections.heading: Rename through VS Code
sections.text: KDataForge Tools can plan a content-ID rename across the selected pack's YAML plus statically provable TypeScript references. It rechecks document versions, exact old text, normalized identity collisions, and a complete pack snapshot before applying one WorkspaceEdit. Dynamic expressions, external packs, aliases, redirects, includes, incomplete inventories, pack refs, and config IDs are refused. You still add and retain the redirects: entry described above when a shipped generated ID changes. - Shipped an id rename, then got reports of missing items in old saves: you forgot the redirects: entry. Add it retroactively in a follow-up version. It's read fresh at every load, never baked into the save, so adding it late still fixes existing saves the next time they load. No save wipe needed. - Added a redirect, but old saves still show a missing class: check direction and spelling first. The map is OldId: NewId, not the reverse, and both sides are the raw id: value (not the display name), matched exactly. SanitizeToken only swaps non-alphanumeric characters for underscores, so it doesn't fix a typo or a case mismatch. - How to verify a redirect took effect: ApplyRedirects logs one line per entry to the game log at Log severity (visible without enabling KDF.Debug): [LogKDataForge] Redirect: /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_OldId -> /KDataForge/Gen/MyPack.Gen_MyPack_NewId. /kdf report shows load diagnostics (errors/warnings/tombstones) but doesn't list applied redirects directly, so the log is the source of truth here. - Accidentally renamed a pack ref: there's no redirect fix (see above). The practical options are reverting the ref back, or accepting that saves made before the change lose those generated objects. They'll come back as tombstones with a warning if the old ref's YAML still exists somewhere, otherwise they're gone. The generated class identity contract is the normative persistence reference. Conditions & Packs has the compact redirects: syntax, while End-to-End Pack shows the same rename inside a complete multi-file pack.

pages.title: Custom research trees
pages.description: Build a named M.A.M. research tree and place a MAM-type schematic in its visual node graph entirely from YAML.

sections.heading: Custom research trees
sections.text: KDataForge can generate and register a M.A.M. research tree, create MAM-type schematics, and place those schematics in the tree's visual graph. You can extend an existing tree or remove a branch without leaving dangling graph links. This workflow does not require Unreal Editor. Use type: research (or the filename-convention alias mam, such as my-tree.mam.yml).

sections.heading: Step 1: create the tree
sections.text: # file: kdf-sample.research.yml type: research research: - id: KDFSampleTree properties: mDisplayName: KDF Sample Research mPreUnlockDisplayName: '???' mPreUnlockDescription: Complete the HUB milestone that reveals this tree. mPostUnlockDescription: Research refined ingot processing. This generates a real UFGResearchTree subclass. register: true, the default, queues it into SML's UModContentRegistry. The pre-unlock fields appear before the tree is revealed; the normal display name and post-unlock description appear afterward.

sections.heading: Step 2: create a MAM-type schematic
sections.text: mType: EST_MAM uses the same generation, registration, cost, and unlocks: mechanisms as a HUB milestone. It marks the schematic as research: # file: pure-super-ingot.schematic.yml type: schematic schematics: - id: Schematic_PureSuperIngot properties: mType: EST_MAM mDisplayName: Refined Ingot Processing mDescription: Research a purer smelting process for the Super Ingot. mTechTier: 1 mTimeToComplete: 30 mCost: - ItemClass: /Game/FactoryGame/Resource/Parts/IronPlateReinforced/Desc_IronPlateReinforced.Desc_IronPlateReinforced_C Amount: 10 unlocks: - class: /Game/FactoryGame/Unlocks/BP_UnlockRecipe.BP_UnlockRecipe_C properties: mRecipes: - /KDataForge/Gen/KDFSample.Gen_KDFSample_Recipe_PureSuperIngot Build the item and recipe behind this schematic with the pattern from Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock.

sections.heading: Step 3: place the schematic in the tree
sections.text: Add addNodes: to the research entry. Each entry creates an instanced research-tree node: # file: kdf-sample.research.yml type: research research: - id: KDFSampleTree properties: mDisplayName: KDF Sample Research mPreUnlockDisplayName: '???' mPreUnlockDescription: Complete the HUB milestone that reveals this tree. mPostUnlockDescription: Research refined ingot processing. addNodes: - schematic: Schematic_PureSuperIngot coordinate: X: 0 Y: 0 KDataForge creates the shared base-game BPD_ResearchTreeNode, writes the schematic and coordinate into its Blueprint data struct, and appends it to the tree's mNodes array.

sections.heading: Step 4: add prerequisites and roads
sections.text: Reference another node by schematic id in parents:. Set autoPath: true on the research entry to generate straight roads automatically: type: research research: - id: KDFSampleTree autoPath: true properties: mDisplayName: KDF Sample Research addNodes: - schematic: Schematic_PureSuperIngot coordinate: X: 0 Y: 0 - schematic: Schematic_PureSuperIngotAdvanced coordinate: X: 1 Y: 0 parents: - schematic: Schematic_PureSuperIngot References can point forward or backward in the same addNodes: list because KDataForge records all coordinates before resolving relationships. It also indexes nodes that already exist on the target tree. Following example adds one node to vanilla Mycelia tree; register: false prevents redundant content-registry registration while still applying node mutation: type: research research: - class: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Research/Mycelia_RS/ResearchTree_Mycelia.ResearchTree_Mycelia_C register: false autoPath: true addNodes: - schematic: Schematic_MyExtension coordinate: X: 4 Y: 2 parents: - schematic: Schematic_ExistingParent nodesToUnhide: - X: 5 Y: 2 nodesToUnhide: and unhiddenBy: use the same literal-coordinate or block-map schematic: reference form as parents:. A custom UFGResearchTreeNode subclass can be selected with class:; use its properties: mapping for any additional reflected fields. For a custom route, keep autoPath: false and define childrenAndRoads: on the parent: addNodes: - schematic: Schematic_PureSuperIngot coordinate: X: 0 Y: 0 childrenAndRoads: key: X: 1 Y: 0 points: - X: 0 Y: 0 - X: 0 Y: 1 - X: 1 Y: 1 - X: 1 Y: 0 See the addNodes: schema for nodesToUnhide:, unhiddenBy:, multiple children, and custom node classes.

sections.heading: Step 5: add, remove, or move nodes safely
sections.text: Use tree-entry-level removeNodes: when a branch is no longer part of your pack. Select each node by its schematic class; a generated short id works when it resolves unambiguously. Put addNodes: beside it to add a replacement or another branch in the same mutation. autoPath: true generates roads for newly added parent relationships: type: research research: - class: /Game/FactoryGame/Schematics/Research/Mycelia_RS/ResearchTree_Mycelia.ResearchTree_Mycelia_C autoPath: true removeNodes: - Schematic_ObsoleteExtension addNodes: - schematic: Schematic_NewExtension coordinate: X: 6 Y: 3 parents: - schematic: Schematic_ExistingParent KDataForge removes the selected node and cleans every surviving reference to its coordinate: Parents, NodesToUnhide, UnhiddenBy, and ChildrenAndRoads. In one tree entry, removals run before the new addNodes: list is appended, so example above removes obsolete branch before adding new one. Omit addNodes: when node should disappear completely. To move or replace a node, use same schematic in both lists and give addNodes: entry its new coordinate. Legacy nodes: remains accepted, but addNodes: wins when both keys exist.

sections.heading: How the Blueprint node data is writable
sections.text: The base C++ node exposes GetNodeSchematic() as a BlueprintImplementableEvent. The shared BPD_ResearchTreeNode class also stores its data in the Blueprint variable mNodeDataStruct. KDataForge resolves the struct's authored member names through reflection, including Blueprint members whose internal storage names contain GUIDs. This is the same property-resolution mechanism used elsewhere in KDataForge. A custom UFGResearchTreeNode subclass can be selected with class: and can receive extra operations through the node's properties: mapping.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - The tree does not appear: Confirm register: true and inspect /kdf report. - A node field is missing: Check /kdf report or KDF.Debug 1 for an unresolved schematic or authored field name. - A custom class: fails: It must derive from UFGResearchTreeNode. - Automatic roads are not shaped correctly: autoPath only creates straight two-point roads. Use manual childrenAndRoads: for bends. - The MAM schematic is not purchasable: Verify its cost item, registration, and unlock classes. The Research Trees and Schematics feature pages explain the two capabilities independently. The node schema is the normative field reference. If the item, recipe, and schematic chain is new to you, start with Item + Icon + Recipe + Tier-1 Unlock.

pages.title: Tag-based bulk balancing
pages.description: Register your own gameplay tag, mark a pile of content as yours or as needing rebalancing, and bulk-edit everything carrying that tag in one patch instead of one cdo patch per target.

sections.heading: Tag-based bulk balancing
sections.text: This tutorial creates a reusable tag, applies it to recipes across separate files, and edits all of them with one matchTag: patch. This avoids maintaining a separate target: patch for every recipe. The Balancing example shows the same mechanism in a smaller form.

sections.heading: The problem this solves
sections.text: One target: patch per recipe works fine for three recipes. It stops working once you're maintaining thirty: every new tuned recipe needs its own patch entry, and nothing tells you which recipes are "yours" versus vanilla, untouched ones. A gameplay tag fixes both problems. Tag every recipe you touch as you create or edit it, then write one patch that matches the tag and applies to whatever currently carries it. That covers today's four recipes or next month's forty, with no patch-list maintenance required. > ℹ️ Tags are for sets the game does not already describe. If the recipes you want share a > producer building, an ingredient, a product, a naming convention, or a property value, you don't > need a tag at all: producedIn:, ingredient:, product:, matchName: and where: select on > those directly, and combine with matchTag: on the same patch. See > Targeting → scope filters. > This tutorial is about the case where the set is defined by *you*, not by the data.

sections.heading: Step 1: register your own tag
sections.text: # file: myoverhaul-tags.gametag.yml type: gametag tags: - tag: MyOverhaul.Rebalanced comment: Recipes tuned by MyOverhaul's balance pass Full mechanics are in Game Tags, but the short version matters here. UKDFGameTagHandler does not write a tag .ini file anywhere. Instead it appends a row straight onto the UGameplayTagsSettings CDO's GameplayTagList array, in memory only, never saved to disk, then calls DestroyGameplayTagTree() / ConstructGameplayTagTree() so the engine's tag tree picks it up. That rebuild is what makes FGameplayTag::RequestGameplayTag("MyOverhaul.Rebalanced") resolve to a valid tag afterward. Registration is idempotent, so an already-listed tag is skipped. This needs GameplayTags.ImportTagsFromConfig = true, which Satisfactory ships with enabled, so you don't need to configure anything for that part. GameTags is always the first stage, ahead of every other document type in the same load. That means this tag is already registered and usable by the time any cdo document in the same pack runs, so no include: is needed for the gametag file itself.

sections.heading: Existing content (vanilla or another mod's): a plain `cdo` patch
